There are three features in the foregoing statement worthy of some attention. First, we have the statement of American authorities endorsed, namely: that storage facilities in Canada are better than in the United States. It is not a question of permanence of structures, because the United States is committed to the construction of a dam some forty feet in height, which will probably hold behind it 200,000 feet of wateT. It is a question of putting two holes in the bottom of that dam, one for the use of Canada, the other for the use of the United States. That of course, would involve the building of the American canal as originally located, and involve

that country in greater expense. Instead of that, however, there is to be one hole in that dam twenty-five feet above the river level, out of which the American share of the water will be taken, and the Canadian share of the water will go down the valley uncontrolled.
Then, we have the opinion of Mr. Dennis, that by using the storage facilities of the northern slope of the Milk river, Canada can store all her share of water. That statement is absolutely incorrect. The storage facilities of Canada are situated many miles from the St. Mary's river. They can only be connected by earthen canals with the river. Those cana'ls can only be operated in normal years, about seven months in each year. We must realize that earthen canals must be closed down in order to allow them to dry out, so that teams can be placed in them to do the necessary repairs before the frost sets in. Any child in these northern latitudes knows that water cannot be carried in such canals during the winter months. Then, what happens to the flow of the stream for what, I may term, the five winter months? It is true that water will run longer than seven months, but I have already explained that the canals have to be closed down, and my 'experience in operating canals, is that they have never operated more than about seven months per year. So that at once disposes of that question. Then the other statement is that the storage in the basin of the St. Mary's lake would be of little or no service to Canada. All I have to say in connection with that is that the storage in the basin of the St. Mary's lake, is good enough for the United States, and, looking carefully over the entire treaty, and the success which has attended the efforts of the United States in its negotiations. I am disposed to think that what is good enough for that country, should be good enough for this.
Sir, when this question was before the House in May, 1909, the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) criticised me rather severely for importing, as he said, political bias into this debate. I absolutely deny the charge, Sir. I was not sent here to throw platitudes at anv one in this House. I came here to look after what I regard as the interests of the people of this country. I went into the western country over thirty years ago, without any very great appreciation of the value of either water or timber. I settled on the plains of western Canada, and it gradually came to me the great value of these two natural advantages. I was connected with development work in southern Alberta, and I say that any man who has an interest in this country 288
should be glad to take part in making two blades of grass grow where one grew before I realize the necessity, as the people in that country to-day realize the necessity of every drop of water we are entitled to. We know that we have not sufficient water for our needs; and when the government allows water to be taken from us to which we are legally entitled, I have every right to come here to criticise the government. More than that, Sir, we are not doing what I consider we should do in the development of the water resources of that country. We have vast bodies of water going down towards Hudson bay, and doing little or no good. The government should carry on careful investigations to see to what extent the water can be put to beneficial use. Nothing is now being done in that direction beyond the measurement of some streams. But, before we can attempt the development of our water resources other things need to be done. We have certain gentlemen north of Lethbridge asking that water should be taken out of the Belly river for use in that country. They are not in a position to say whether that is or is not feasible from an engineering point of view. The government ought to go to their aid and tell them to what extent it is feasible.
Now, a few words dealing more closely with the Bill before us-that is in reference to the appointment of the three gentlemen who will be associated with the three appointees of the United States for operating the Waterways Treaty. I understand that the three representatives of the United States were selected several weeks ago and that ex-Senator Carter, of Montana, is one of them. Senator Carter was most active and aggressive in pushing forward Montana's claims during negotiation of the treaty.
I consider that our government has a great opportunity to render a signal service to Canada in the selection of the three Canadian representatives. In my opinion, it is not a question of obtaining gentlemen with legal lore, as the questions which will be involved are engineering questions. We know that continental Europe has been forced through circumstances to reduce transportation to a science. She has been forced to bring her water routes-the very cheapest-to the highest point of development. She has developed energy for industrial purposes in the same way, and in doing so, has made use of electricity for the transmission of power produced from water. Irrigation with her has likewise been brought to the highest point of efficiency, therefore, her engineers have had greater opportunity than has yet been offered in young America, but America is being forced in the same direction, through keen competition. Then, it appears to me that this is



the time for Canada to hunt for a man who stands pre-eminent in that branch of the engineering profession, which this commission will be called upon to deal with, namely, water questions. L'et us get that man, regardless of price or where he comes from,as we need a man with such a reputation that when he speaks he will be listened to throughout Europe as well as America. Having secured such a man, let our government place a copy of the treaty in his hands with instructions to carry on investigations along the international boundary, so that when the five-year period for which the treaty was made comes- to an end, he will be able to point out all the weak places so far as Canada is concerned. Place before him a map of Canada and draw his attention to the vast bodies of water possessed by this country, with streams flowing in almost every direction; point out to him the strategic position this country possesses in the world of commerce, and the vast quantities of raw materials we possess. Tell him to study Canada's problems of industrial development so as to be able to lay down a policy of water-power development and water transportation that will permit this country to get its products into the markets of the world at the lowest possible figure. Then, Sir, every link that we lay down in our transportation system will be -a link in that enlarged plan of'our ultimate aim in the matter of transportation which will enable Canada to be a great country with a prosperous people.

speakeroldname: Hon. FRANK OLIVER (Minister of the Interior).
speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am sure the House has listened very attentively to my hon. friend from Medicine Hat (Mr. Magrath). No member of the House is better qualified to speak on the general question of the rights to water and the uses of water, and nobody is better qualified to speak on the question dealt with in article 6 of the treaty, than is my hon. friend. Therefore, it is right, first that he should give every attention to the matter, and next that the House should give every attention to him. He has marshalled his arguments and his facts very well. The only criticism that I would have to offer is that my hon. friend has proved too much. He has proved, in his opinion, that the government has been absolutely derelict in its duty, has paid no attention to- the rights of the people, has ignored the facts, and generally has thrown away an opportunity to protect the interests particularly of the constituency he represents. I am sure the House will forgive me if I do not agree in that extreme view. I shall not endeavour to follow my hon. friend through the technicalities of the subject, and I have no fault to find with the way in which he has presented the facts. What I criticise is his deductions from these facts, and I think I Mr. MAGRATH.
can show the House, from the hon. gentleman's own figures, that his deductions are not by any means warranted.
The position with regard to the matters dealt with in article six is exactly as he has stated. There are two rivers which take their rise in the United States, and flow into Canada. The smaller flows out of Canada back into the United States, and the larger remains in Canada, and flows into Hudson bay. The arrangement whereby Canada has granted three-quarters of the flow of these rivers in low water and one-half in high water, he condemns as an improvident one. I admit at once that, as compared with an arrangement which would secure to Canada the whole flow of both streams, it would be an improvident arrangement. But that was not the alternative. Let me put the alternative as I understand it, and as the House will understand it from what my hon. friend has said. The alternative was not between securing one-half of the water of the two streams and all the water, but between securing one-half of the water of the two and none of it, speaking of their low water flow. If the House has followed my hon. friend's statement, it will recollect that the proposition of the United States government, and the Reclamation Commission was to divert the whole of the low water flow, and some part of the high water flow of the St. Mary's river from its natural channel, out of its -own drainage basin, into the drainage basin of the Milk river.

But what right had they to do anything of the kind? That is an international stream, taking its (rise in the United 'States and flowing through Canadian territory into Hudson bay. I have yet to find any authority for the proposition that the United States had the right to do anything of the kind.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I take exactly the same view as my hon. friend, but I think he will agree with me that, if they had not the right, beyond question they had the power to do it, and that was what was in question.
My hon. friend says they have the power to do it. They have diverted the St. Mary's river into the Milk river south of the boundary line.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They have not done so, but propose doing so.
Well, there is nothing to prevent this government diverting the water of the Milk river into the St. Mary's.

I understand the hon. minister to say that undoubtedly the Unit-

ed States had not the right to divert this water.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In my opinion they had not.
But they had the power. In what way had they the power? Was it by force?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They had the power because the water originated within their territory and they were able to make a diversion of it within their own territory; and as a sovereign power, not governed at that time by any treaty, there is no doubt that whatever the right may be, the power absolutely lay with them to make that diversion and take the whole low water flow of the St. Mary's out of the drainage basin of the St. Mary's, and thereby leave all my hon. friend's constituents high and dry, so far as the low water flow of the St. Mary's was concerned, he will not dispute that statement.
Why did you not offer a counter proposition?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This is a counter proposition, but I wish to deal further with the suggestion of my hon. friend from North Simcoe. The proposition of the United States government was to divert the water of the St. Mary's into the Milk river, and then use the Milk river as a channel whereby that water could be taken around to Montana, and then used on the lands contiguous to the Milk river.
That would pass through miles of Canadian territory.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Precisely, we all agree as to the facts. This Milk river passes for 100 miles through Canadian territory, and the level was such that it was possible for Canada to tap that Milk river within Canadian territory and thereby take from it the water that would be taken out of the St. Mary's. As a matter of fact a ditch was dug for that purpose, but it would not take the water onto the land owned by the settlers in whose behalf my hon. friend (Mr. Ma-grath) was speaking.

Yes, it would. The hon. minister will pardon me for contradicting him. I gave the contract for the portion of the Milk river ditch, and must know something about it. The water could be brought to Raymond and northward.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I would not care to enter into a controversy with my hon. friend on an engineering question.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Could it be secured to the town named after my hon. friend?
No, there is very little water distributed there.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon. friend says that, so far as a large part of the lands occupied by his constituents is concerned, this wateT could be taken out of the Milk river and distributed along that land, but to a part of that land it could not. My excuse for assuming that the water could not be brought from the Milk river into the St. Mary's direct is because at present if, flows from the St. Mary's direct into the Milk river. While the possibility exists to take out of the Milk river what might have been taken out of the St. Mary's, and put into it by the United States, there is the further possibility that the United States did not need to do that. They could have carried the water of the St. Mary's river past the Milk river into another river which did not flow through Canada, and could thereby have defeated the purpose that was in the mind of the hon. member for Simcoe when he said that if they put the water into the Milk riveT we could take it out again. Thev did not need to put the water into the Milk river, they could have put it into another river, and could have used the water of that river. True, that would not have been an economical proposition, it would have cost more than it was worth. But it is an engineering fact that it could have been done, and, it is a financial fact that the United States has money enough to do it. Speaking from my place in parliament, I would not like to go further and suggest that sometimes it has appeared to me that the United States is not always governed by economical considerations in dealing with a neighbouring country. At any Tate, I have placed the situation before the House. The choice was not between getting half the water and all the water, it was between getting half the water and none at all, therefore, the government of Canada took the course that is laid down in the treaty as being in the best interests of the people concerned. We were not in a position absolutely to protect their interests, therefore, we believe that we were well advised in protecting them as far as we were able. That this action of ours was well taken I am convinced from the fact that we have an assurance from the head of the responsible company which to-day owns the irrigation rights that my hon. friend has spoken about, that is to say, the residuary rights which have not yet been disposed

of, and the head of this company advised the government that the company was satisfied with the arrangement that was then about to be made. Under these circumstances, while I am free to admit that the arrangement was not such as we would have liked to make, and that perhaps we might have made a more favourable arrangement with our neighbours, still it was such an arrangement as commended itself, under all the circumstances, to the people who were most directly financially interested, as well as to the government, in dealing with what was a very, very difficult question. I just wish to sav that I think my hon. friend was not justified in the conclusions that he drew from the very accurate statement of facts that he made. I do not think the government have slighted the interests of the people affected, and are not to be blamed, but rather they are entitled to credit for having done all that could have been done, under the difficult circumstances, to protect those interests.

speakeroldname: Mr. C. J. DOHERTY (Montreal, St. Anne).
speechtext:
In this Bill there seems to be a very material change from the provisions of the Bill when it was originally introduced. The Minister of Public Works told us this morning, if I followed him correctly, that he had introduced some new sections for the purpose of making it clear that there should be a jurisdiction in the courts of this country to try actions contemplated by the treaty brought by persons residing in the United States. It seems to me that the first section of this amended Act modifies materially the case, and puts this House, as towards this Bill, in a_. very different position from that which it occupied at the time the Bill was originally introduced. By the first section of the amended Act this Bill purports to confirm, and sanction the treaty that was made. Now if I understand the situation, when the Bill was originally introduced, the treaty was considered as being absolutely in force and binding upon us, and what parliament was asked to do was to provide for the officers to be named under the treaty, for their appointment, and for their fees. The Bill now seems to proceed upon the principle that the treaty requires some confirmation, or some sanction from this House; because I do not suppose that the government is asking us to go through a performance which is absolutely unnecessary, which can have no effect. It would appear now that the government must be under some impression that this parliament has power to deal with the treaty in the shape of ratifying it, and I suppose that if we can ratify we would likewise have the right to refuse our ratification. Perhaps the_ minister will say whether he understands by this clause of the Bill that a Mr. OLIVER
confirmation of this treaty by parliament is necessary.

I thought I had made it clear that it is the opinion of the Department of Justice that, in order to give authority to a court to subpoena witnesses and to have them sworn before giving their testimony, an Act of this parliament is necessary; also, that legislation is required in order to give a right to American citizens to proceed in the courts of this country pursuant to the terms of the treaty. That 's the object of introducing the legislation. Of course, in doing that it is desirable that we should ratify the whole treaty, because these clauses are essential parts of it.

I can understand that the sections following section 1 do make provisions for the machinery to enforce the yights that are created under the treaty. But section 1 purports purely, and simply to sanction and confirm the treaty. Now it seems to me that one of two things must be true ; either the treaty requires a sanction and ratification by this parliament, and we have power to sanction and ratify it, which also implies that we have power to refuse to sanction or ratify it; or the treaty requires no sanction or confirmation on our part, and we have no power to confirm or to refuse to confirm. Now, if the latter is the case, the government is asking this parliament to put itself into a position where it subjects itself to the criticism that it is undertaking to deal with a matter with which it has no possible concern.	,
What would be the effect upon this treaty if parliament refused to pass this Bill? Surely the first inference would be that the treaty was not binding upon it, and it seems to me that we ought to be very careful before we undertake to break into a matter with which we have no right to deal. I have understood up to the present that the position that the government took was that this treaty was completely binding upon us as soon as it was passed, and that we had no further power in the matter than to provide machinery to carry it out. The introduction of this section raises a very important question. If I understand it rightly, the treaty-making power is vested in the Crown, and it seems to me that if this be a treaty which can be made by the Crown without any intervention of any other authority, it is nothing short of a piece of impertinence on our part to take it upon ourselves to sanction or confirm it. If, on the other hand, this be a treaty which can only become binding upon its ratification by parliament, then I entirely fail to see how this parliament comes to be the proper body which ought to pronounce that ratification. I do not want to go into a discussion of this matter in detail of whether ratifica-

tion is necessary or not, but it seems to me that if it be a case *where ratification is necessary this parliament is without power to deal with this question of ratification. I understand there are treaties which are recognized as requiring legislative action to make them perfectly and completely binding, and that among treaties of that kind are those which have the effect of modifying or altering the private rights of individuals which require legislative action to make them binding upon those individuals. But, in that view, so long as the treaty-making power is exercised by His Majesty, not as forming any part of the parliament of Canada, but His Majesty as being the King of Great Britain and Ireland, and, therefore, Sovereign of the empire, it seems to me that the only legislative body, which, under these circumstances if we assume ratification to be necessary to this treaty, could take upon itself, or would be the body, to exercise that power would be the imperial parliament and not this parliament here at all. I do not know that the British North America Act gives us any treaty-making power of any kind, and if ratification is essential to this treaty then the pronouncement of the ratification is a part of the making of the treaty. I quite understand that it might have been a part of the treaty that it should be subject to ratification by this parliament, and if that had been so then I quite understand that it would be within the purview of this parliament to pronounce upon it and say whether it would confirm and ratify it or not. But. there is nothing of the kind in the treaty; so that, it seems to me that by this first section the government is asldng parliament to do a something which it has absolutely no power, or no quality, or no function to do. I do not know whether the answer would be that even if it is none of our business it would not do any harm if we should do this. I do not think that is a very conclusive answer because I do think that this parliament ought to guard itself against laying itself open to the accusation of stepping in where it has no power to ratify or refuse to ratify What His Majesty, in the exercise of his prerogative powers, has done, because stepping in to r.aitify does imply that it lies with us, if we choose, to refuse to ratify this treaty. Now, if it be assumed-and I suppose we must assume it, inasmuch as the government asks us to ratify this treaty-that we have some power in the matter, and that it is open to us to refuse to ratify this treaty if we choose, then, it seems to me the question arises- and I believe it is a very important question-as to whether we ought to ratify this treaty. I think that my hon. friend from Medicine Hat (Mr. Magrath) made out a strong case this morning in regard to one
feature indicating that we should refuse to ratify the treaty. An important clause of 'the Bid] is that Which purports to grant the right of action 'against individuals in this country for damages resulting from diversions iof streams running 'through this fcountry, and that ultimately pass into the United States. In that regard it seems to me that the government, by this treaty, has undertaken to create rights, of action against individuals in the different provinces and then, because it has taken upon itself to create these rights of action, follows it up in this measure by withdrawing the individuals who may be responsible for such diversions, and who are consequently subjected to the rights of action the treaty purports to create, from their natural jurisdiction before . the provincial courts and making them amenable to the Exchequer Court and liable to be brought away from their homes and the jurisdiction of their courts 'which are constitutionally charged with the administration of the civil law to answer for what after all is on their part a violation of the civil law, or the common law, as the case may be, giving rise to action in damages on the part of persons who have suffered by it. The provision of the treaty is this. It is agreed that:
Any interference with or diversion from their natural channel of any waters in Canada, which in their natural channels would flow across the boundary between Canada and the United States or into boundary waters (as defined in the said treaty) resulting in any injury on the United States side of the boundary, shall give the same rights and entitle the injured parties to the same legal remedies as if such injury took place in that part of Canada where such diversion or interference occurs, but this section shall not apply to eases existing on the eleventh day of January, one thousand nine hundred and nine, or to cases expressly covered by special agreement between His Majesty and the government of the United States.
I understand that the purpose _of this article is to give to persons in the United States suffering from the diversions of streams that take place in this country the same right of action which a person living in this country would have against a person who is responsible for the diversion. If that is correct, the right of action that is created or recognized in favour of this outsider is a right of action that is governed bv the'law of the province in which the diversion takes place. It does not appear to be intended to give an outsider any greater right of action than exists already in the country in which the diversion takes place as between the person responsible for that diversion and the person who has suffered damage. The right of action, therefore, is a right of action which results from the common law or the civil law, as the case may be, in the particular province in which the

One or two words before the treaty passes. In the first place I desire to extend my congratulations to the hon. member for Medicine Hat for the very able and lucid address he has gjiven to the House to-day, in which he has set forth very distinctly the practical effect of this treaty, from his standpoint, upon the conditions in the province of Alberta and more particularly in connection with the waters of the St. Mary's river and the Milk river. The hon. member (Mr. Magrath) has gone into the matter with very great thoroughness. He has reviewed the situation from beginning to end in a very fair and convincing manner and in my opinion he has demonstrated very completely that the government, in negotiating this treaty, have not taken the best means of safeguarding the interests of the people of Canada, and have not adequately safeguarded these interests. T would like to say to the Minister of Public Works who has charge of the Bill, that during the period which has intervened between the signing of this treaty and the present time the situation has been to some extent altered if we may judge by what has recently been to the fore in the way of negotiations between the government of Great Britain and the government of the United States for a general arbitration treaty.
I do not think that the President of the United States can be too highly commended

for the position he has taken in that respect, and I would like to quote to the House the language he used in what has been called his inspired deliverance before the peace and arbitration society in New York on the 22nd March, 1910. He said:
Personally I do not see any more reason why matters of national honour should not be referred to a court of arbitration than matters of property or of national proprietorship. I know that is going farther than most men are willing to go, but I do not see why questions of honour may not be submitted to a tribunal composed of men of honour who understand questions of national honour, to abide by their decision as well as any other question of difference arising between nations.
We all know that up to the present time treaties of arbitration between the nations [DOT]of the earth have excepted matters (which concern the national honour, or the vital interests of either country. President Taft took a memorable step in advance when he used these words I have cited. The policy which he then expressed himself as willing to follow will make his presidency memorable in the history fof the United States, and in the history of the world. But he did something more than that. On the 17th day of December, 1910, he delivered an address at the banquet of the American Society for the Judicial Settlement of International Disputes. [DOT]There iare la great many peace societies in the United States, and the society which I have just named is one which has done most excellent work in the cause of peace throughout the world. In the course of his address on that occasion President Taft went one step further. He said this:
If, now, we can negotiate and put through a positive agreement with some'great nation to abide the ajudicaltion of an international arbitral court in every issue which oan not be settled by negotiation, no matter what it involves, whether honour, territory or money, we shall have made a long step forward by demonstrating that it is possible for two nations at least to establish as between them the same system of due process of law that exists between individuals under a government.
After the two speeches of Mr. Taft, from which I have briefly quoted, it was generally recognized, I think, throughout tth-e world, ittua/t .the .address delivered iby jhim on December 17 last, was practically an invitation or suggestion to Great Britain that the United States would be willing to enter into a treaty of arbitration along those lines with the British Empire.
On the 28th day of April last, a notable gathering assembled at the Guildhall, when the Prime Minister of Great Britain, and the Right Hon. A. J. Balfour, the leader of the opposition in the imperial House of [DOT]Commons, both spoke on this question. I
do not intend to quote from them at any length. Just one or two words from the address of Mr. Asquith on that occasion:
Arbitration for the settlement of disputes between nations is already familiar to us, but hitherto points of national honour of vital importance have been reserved and have not been referred to courts of arbitration. Now, whatever the magnitude of the interest may be, whatever poignancy of feeling may be involved, war will be absolutely abandoned.
Then he went on to say further:
It is the privilege of great natipns as well as of great men not only to follow but to acknowledge precedents. If the United States and Great Britain make this compact it will be an immeasurable step in the progress of humanity.
Mr. Balfour spoke entirely along the same lines, and in precisely the same spirit.
It is understood that negotiations have been going on for some time between the government of the United States, and the government of His Britannic Majesty along these lines. Of course, it is yet a diplomatic secret as to how far these negotiations may have been advanced. But if they are in good progress, and we have every reason to believe that such is the case, may they not in effect supersede a treaty of this kind, which deals with only one kind of possible dispute between the United States, and a portion of the British Empire alone. I do not, of course, deny that the tribunal would be differently constituted. 'There would be a greater and a stronger itri'bunal under the general arbitration [DOT]treaty now contemplated than the tribunal constituted by this commission; but we 'have nothing to fear, I hope, from that. [DOT]Therefore, it would -be well for us to pause [DOT]for a moment to .consider whether everything that this treaty accomplishes, and a great deal more besides, may not he accomplished by the .arbitration1 treaty that iwe hope will be consummated before veTy Jong. /Besides, isomeithing can. be said for the position that it would be better for Canada to stand in line with the rest of the empire in respect of such a matter than to have its own particular arbitration treaty dealing with its special differences with the United States. It would seem to me that there could not be any possible objection on the part of the United States to that outcome, and certainly there ought not to be any objection on the part (of Canada.
My hoin. friend from St. Anne (Mr. iDoherty) has .spoken of the complete change in this Bill. It is completely changed from the form in which it was presented to parliament in the first instance, because it is now proposed by the first section to ratify the treaty, and by the second sec-

tion to alter anl amend the laws of Canada, and of the several provinces of Canada, so far as may be necessary to carry out and perform the obligations of this treaty. In speaking upon this question in this House on the 14th day of May, 1909, I argued, and I have seen no reason since to change my views, that this treaty should have been made subject to ratification by the Canadian parliament. After examining this question, as discussed in the most recent and authoritative text books I arrived at the conclusion that treaties of the following character should be made subject to the approval of parliament:	First,
those imposing any burden on the people; second, those involving any change in the law of the land; third, those requiring legislative action to make them effective, or which affect the free exercise of the legislative nower; fourth, those affecting territorial rights. I pointed out also that Anson, in his work upon the British constitution, referred in the edition of 1896 to the Heligoland Treaty between Great Britain and Germany as creating an unfortunate 'precedent. In that case Great Britain, having ceded the Island of Heligoland, subject to the approval of parliament, came to parliament for ratification of the treaty. It was at that time apparently the view of the British government that any treaty involving the cession of territory ought to 'be made subject to the approval of parliament. Anson, in his edition of 1896, criticised this as an unfortunate precedent. In his edition of 1908 he withdraws that criticism and says this:
We seem to be drawn to this conclusion, that apart from precedents relating to Indian territory, it has of recent years been thought desirable, if not necessary, that the consent of parliament should be given to the cession of territory in time of peace.
I pointed out also that Lowell, in his recent work on the government of England, at page 22 of volume 1, used this language:
The Crown has power to declare war, make peace and conclude treaties, save that, without the sanction of parliament, a treaty cannot impose a charge upon the people or change the law of the land, and it is doubtful how far without that sanction private rights can be sacrificed or territory ceded.
Then there are a great many recent treaties between Great Britain and foreign countries which have been made subject to the ratification of the British parliament.
I need not go over these again. It appears now that the Minister of Justice (Sir Allen Aylesworth), according to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley), has come to the conclusion that this treaty must be ratified by parliament. That is (perfectly obvious, as I pointed out most (distinctly in May, 1909, but could not then Mr. BORDEN (Halifax). '
find any one on the treasury 'benches -wfill-*ing to agree with me. I then said:
This treaty must have the effect of altering the law of the land if carried into effect. Y^ou must have new laws in regard to actions brought by people in Canada against people residing in the United States, or by people in the United States against people domiciled in Canada.
And I argued, as I claim to-day, that it cannot be carried into effect without the ratification of parliament. My hon. friend the member for St. Anne division (Mr. Doherty), has shown the singular situation into which the matter has been brought by the action of the government. They did not make this treaty subject to the ratification of any parliament. They took the ground, contrary to all British precedents in the last twenty years, that this treaty need not be made subject to the ratification of parliament, but still they come to-day, and ask parliament to ratify it. In taking that step they are, therefore, departing from the position they took in the first instance. Inasmuch as this treaty was not made subject to the ratification of any parliament, what has this parliament to do with ratifying it to-day? In the absence of any provision in the treaty itself, there is strong ground for the argument which my hon. friend from St. Anne-has presented, that the proner parliament tp ratify it is the British parliament. Before the hon. gentleman reads that-did not this water commission decide that according to international law and custom the tributary waters of the Rainy river which flow down to the boundary could not be diverted southward to Duluth?

The fundamental principle of international law is the absolute sovereignty of every nation, as against all others, within its own territory. What is the view which Great Britain takes of the rights of a country to deal with waters in its own territory? I have only to call attention to what took place in my own province some forty or fifty years ago. There was a river called the Allegash flowing from a lake called Chamberlain lake through a portion of the United States into the river St. John. About forty years ago the people in the state of Maine under the authority of the legislature of that state erected a dam at the foot of Chamberlain lake the result of which was to turn back the waters of the watershed from the St. John river to the Penobscot, and so send the waters down through the state of Maine into the Atlantic ocean in the vicinity I think, of Bangor. The result of that was to enable the lumbermen of that section of country, instead of sending the logs down the Allegash to the St. John and thereby to the city of St. John and other towns on the river St. John for manufacturing, to turn them down the Penobscot, an American river entirely, and manufacture them in their own country. The government of New Brunswick sent a protest through the British Ambassador to the British government. We protested year after year. Some of those interested in lumbering on the upper waters of the Allegash, and I think that upon one occasion they blew up the dam, but it was restored again by those who had erected it. There came pretty nearly being bloodshed as the result of what was deemed to be an infringement of the rights of the people along the St. John river. After confederation protests were again made.
Is any part of the Allegash in our territory?
No.
It is all in Maine?

All in the United States, but it flows into the St. John river, which
is a boundary river between the two countries. The water of the Allegash, in a state of nature, flows first into the St. John where it is the boundary, and a certain distance below that it is wholly within New Brunswick territory. Therefore, it was water which, in its natural state, flowed into Canadian waters. After confederation protests were again put in by the New Brunswick government. These protests were sent to His Excellency the Governor General here who transmitted them to the British Ambassador at Washington, and they were transmitted by the British Ambassador to the British government. Although these complaints had been made, and although these protests were vigorously supported during the long time which has elapsed, forty years, the British government have never felt that this was a case in which they could take issue with the United States, but they have recognized that the government of the state of Maine, with the permission of the federal government, were exercising the right of sovereignty within their own country.
They are our neighbours.
Yes, they are our dearest friends.

If the British government, for whose opinions, or course of action, we have the greatest possible respect acquiesced in that view of the sovereign rights of the people of the United States I am inclined to think that we would hesitate before we would be inclined to say that they were wrong.
Have they acquiesced?
Certainly, because they have allowed that to be done for forty years without taking any effective measures to prevent them from continuing it.

Now, can you conceive of a better arrangement for the people of Alberta, who are interested in this irrigation question, than is made in that provision? That provision was not in the suggestion of the American government made by Secretary Root. It was put into the treaty after lengthy negotiations, after our representatives and myself had urged upon those representing the United States, that it would not be fair to our people unless we could secure a prior right to appropriate a certain quantity of the water of the St. MaTy's river; and after these negotiations the United States agreed to this demand, which is of infinite value to the people

of that section of the province of Alberta. And yet my hon. friend deals with the matter just as if this provision were of no importance. I say it is of enormous importance, because no matter whether the flow of water is great or small, no matter whether the season is exceptionally dry or not, no matter whether little water may be left to the United States or not, we during the irrigation season have up to 500 cubic feet per second, or at least up to three-fourths of the natural flow of the St. Mary's river.

Did I understand the hon. minister to say some time ago that Canada could have the use of some of the diverted waters of the St. Mary's river after they had been turned into the channel of the Milk river?

What I said was this: that is a matter that rests wholly with the commissioners. It is the duty and power of the commissioners to divide all the waters of both rivers, and of all their tributaries equally between the people of the two countries. They can give more of one river to one country and vice versa in respect of the other river; and if in the judgment of the commissioners it would be better to give to the people of Canada a greater portion of the flow of the Milk river, and less of the St. Mary's river, they would have a perfect right to do that. The treaty imposes upon them the duty of dividing the waters of both rivers, treating them as one stream, equally between the people of the two countries, and gives them the power of so distributing the waters as to make the distribution as beneficial as possible to the people of both countries.
Something has been said by my hon. friend with reference to a letter which I wrote to the Prime Minister to be forwarded to Washington, urging that the United States government should undertake to build a dam upon the St. Mary's river for the joint benefit of both countries. I am free to admit that when I wrote that letter I was strongly impressed with the desirability of securing some such arrangement if I could do so. I do not think it will be improperly disclosing any secret if I say that the Canadian government were prepared to pay a portion of the cost of erecting that dam upon American territory; but the government of the United States said, and we cannot perhaps wonder at their saying so, that they would hesitate to accept a contribution from another government for the erection of works in their country, even though they might be irrigation works that would be for the benefit of both countries. But the strong argument they made, as will appear from the correspondence, was that until they had erected a dam, and had some experience whe-Mr. PUGSLEY.
ther or not it would stand in the bed of the St. Mary's river, it would not be desirable to enter into such an arrangement. It will also appear from the correspondence that they argued that it was not practicable to take water from the bed of the river, but that it would have to be taken from a height of about 30 feet above the bed, and therefore, it would not be possible to store more than one-half the water of the river. That was their view. We were not able to make an answer to that, and after careful inquiry we came to the conclusion that on the Canadian side of the line there were opportunities to store the water off St. Mary's river as good as, if not superior, to those on the American side. We gave a great deal of thought to this question of article 6. A good many months intervened before wre finally agreed to the treaty, even after it had been ratified by the United States Senate, We weTe making inquiry with regard to the effect of article 6, looking at it from every possible standpoint, and conferring with those who had a knowledge of the subject. As a result of all this inquiry, we came to the conclusion that it would be in the interest of Canada to sign this treaty, and that on the whole article 6 would be just to the people of Alberta. We did not act upon the judgment of our own experts alone. My hon. friend has stated that the making of this treaty was a breach of faith with the Alberta Railway and Irrigation Company. He made a strong point of that. Well, Sir, when I tell you that the Alberta Railway and Irrigation Company, through Sir Thomas Shaughnessy, the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, which controls more than 60 per cent of the stock of that irrigation company, approved and expressed to us their approval of the execution of this treaty, I think you will hardly be disposed to agree with my hon. friend from Medicine Hat that there was any breach of faith towards that company. We conferred not only with Sir Thomas Shaughnessy, but with Mr. J. S. Dennis of the irrigation department of the Canadian Pacific railway, a gentleman of large experience in irrigation work. I think, Mr. Speaker, that I can now very well pass away from the St. Mary's and Milk rivers, and I will make one or two remarks with regard to what was said by my hon. friend from Montreal, St. Anne (Mr. Doherty), with reference to the Bill itself. He says that he is inclined to think that we have no right to ask this House to confirm and sanction, as section 1 proposes to do, the treaty which has been entered into. I think that we have a clear right to do so. That right is contained in article 12 of the treaty which provides that:
The commission shall have power to administer oaths to witnesses and to take evidence on oath whenever deemed necessary in any proceeding or inquiry, or matter within the jurisdiction under this treaty, and all parties interested therein shall be given convenient opportunity to he heard, and the high contracting parties agree to adopt such legislation as may be appropriate and necessary to give the commission the powers above mentioned on each side of the boundary, and to provide for the issue of subpoenas and for con polling the attendance of witnesses in proceedings before the commission.
I am sure that the hon. member for Montreal, St. Anne, could not have been aware of that provision in article 12. That provision gives us power, and this is the only legislature by which that power can be given to make provision as required by the treaty for the purpose of compelling the attendance of witnesses, and of having



them sworn before giving their evidence. Also, it gives us power to make this provision with regard to a citizen of the United States claiming redress in the courts of our own country for any wrong which he mav have suffered by reason of the diversion of water where the injury takes place upon the other side of the line. Therefore, it is clear that it is not only the right, but it is our duty to make those provisions which are contained in the first five paragraphs of the amended Bill. Hon. gentlemen might say that when I introduced the Bill in the first place I should have thought of these things, and had the sections in. I am quite prepared to say that if I had had an opportunity of conferring personally with my Ihon. .friend the Minister of Justice (Sir Allen Ayles-worth), before the Bill was introduced, and talking the matter over with him. it is not at all unlikely that the Bill as introduced would have contained these sections which we are now asking to be placed in the Bill. But, it is absolutely clear that it is our duty to put them. in the Bill in order to give complete effect to the treaty, in so far as the enforcement of rights, and the granting of remedies is concerned as well as the subpoenaing and swearing of witnesses.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I apologize for taking up so much of the time of the House. The matter is one of a good deal of importance, and I thought it not undesirable that I should reply to the observations which, have been made in criticism of this treaty, which I think is one which is not only just to the pejople whose interest* arel affected by the treaty, and more particularly to those who are living in the province of Alberta, but which is a great step forward in the establishment of permanent peace between Great Britain and the United States. My hon. friend, the leader of the opposition, has referred to the proposed general treaty of arbitration which is now pending between the United' State.s and Great Britain. We all sincerely trust that that treaty will be signed, and will become effective and that for all time to conje it will ensure peace between these gregi nations, but I desire to say that in a smaller way the treaty that this House is now called upon to consider is a great step forward in that direction. When we entered upon these negotiations theTe were irritating questions especially between the people of the west with regard to boundary waters. In our western country people living in the vicinity of the town of Raymond connected with the irrigation company had started upon the construction of some works for the diversion of the waters of the Milk river. The United States government had started in upon certain works for the diversion of the waters of the St. Mary's river. There was ground for ill-Hr. PUGSLEY.
feeling, and it is difficult to say what might have been the result if these negotiations had not been entered upon. This treaty makes provision for all questions relating to boundary waters, all questions arising along the boundary, and all questions of whatever kind, and description which may arise between the government of Canada and the government of the United States being referred to a commission. When the larger treaty goes into force it is possible that it may supersede, and take the place of the present one, but this treaty is. for five years, and only for five years, subject, of course, to its being continued, and we trust it will be continued for all time, unless it be superseded by the larger arbitration treaty between the two countries. If that treaty should come into effect, and should take the place of this one no harm can possibly be done by enacting the present treaty. It is necessary that it shall be brought into force, and brought into force at as early a date as possible. There are many questions which are arising from day to day, and which ought to come before a tribunal such as this will be.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext:
This treaty -which we have before us is a portion of a matter that has been subject to negotiations and treaty-making on previous occasions. The principle laid down by the Canadian negotiators for many years was that in making treaties with the United States of America, all questions should be included within the walls of one treaty; that is 'to say, that questions involving navigation, fisheries, waterways and trade were dealt with in one treaty. By dealing with all these questions in one treaty, the negotiators were able to set off one thing against another, enabling this country, as for instance in the treaty of Washington, to secure something as a set-off against things that were demanded by the United States. Unfortunately for this country, we have now an ambassador at Washington who is very strongly pro-American. This country suffered at one time very severely from another ambassador who was pro-American, I refer to Lord Ashburton, previously Mr. Baring, who was the British ambassador in the negotiations that resulted in the famous Ashburton treaty. Now the house of Baring had large pecuniary connections in the United States. It must be evident now to any one reading cold history, that the associations and connections by marriage, and business, and otherwise, which Mr. Baring, or Lord Ashburton, had at that time with the United States, must largely have influenced

9Ifla.
him in his actions. It was indeed a dangerous thing to have appointed him as ambassador to make a treaty between Great Britain and the United States respecting Canada. We all know how this country has suffered from the Ashburton treaty; and without question those of us who have given the matter any study, even the school children in Canada, now ascribe that treaty and the troubles we have had under it, to the fact that Lord Ashburton had large American connections and was more American than British. We have now at Washington another ambassador who is also, I may say, tainted to a large extent in the same way. We know that Mr. Bryce, who has negotiated this treaty, and who seems intent upon negotiating a treaty at every turn of the road, and on every day in the weeli, is the great historian of the United States, and his book on the American Commonwealth is a text book in nearly all the universities of that country. It has a very large sale in the United States, and therefore he is dependent on the goodwill of the Americans both for his fame and for his profits. Now by a very skilful diplomatic process, within recent years we find that the points upon which there has been any difficulty between the United States and Great Britain have been separated, and a distinct treaty has been negotiated to meet each case. We have had a separate treaty dealing with the fisheries, with some other things; we have had a separate treaty dealing with trade. Now a strange thing has occurred with reference to this treaty and that is the fact, as pointed out by the hon. member for St. Anne (Mr. Doherty), that this treaty requires to be ratified by this House.
To my mind every treaty made for and on behalf of Canada should be submitted to this House before it is ratified or confirmed. The question is a very serious one, and one which has been debated in the mother of parliaments whether the government have the right to make a treaty of this kind, and to come to this House and say: We have pledged the honour of the country, the House must accept this treaty, or whether they have the power to make a treaty without any ratification by parliament whatsoever, which is the principle enunciated by the Minister of Public Works here to-day. It was the original intention to pass this treaty without any reference to parliament whatsoever in the matter. The reference was simply to be made to this House to provide the money for these commissioners, and no such thing as the ratification of the treaty was deemed necessary. But, a change has come over the spirit of their dream, and the treaty is submitted to this House in the form of a schedule. Let us see what has occurred, and what is the practice. In the early
days, in the history of the mother country,, previous to the discovery of America, the rule was, when kings were absolute and' parliament had not attained to any strength* or power, such as it has to-day, that the-king made all the treaties and that these-treaties had the force of law. The question,-was fought out on several occasions, but after the revolution a different rule obtained and from the time of William III. on until the early part of this century, no treaty was undertaken by the government of Great Britain without first receiving the sanction of parliament. It has been held by the most eminent authorities that it is. a sound constitutional rule that all treaties should be first passed upon by parliament before they become law. If such were the case, Mr. Chairman, we would not have the spectacle here of the Minister of Finance coming to this House and declaring that the agreement that he made, with the United States, which is purely a convention, has the absolute force of law, that the honour of this House is pledged and that it must become law whether this parliament so desires or not. Mr. Bagehot, who is a well-known constitutional authority. takes the trouble to discuss this question of treaty making in one of his books, and he says this:
Treaties are quite as important as most laws, and to require the elaborate assent of representative assemblies to every word of the law, and not to consult them even as to the essence of the treaty is prima facie ludicrous. In the older forms of the English constitution this may have been quite right; the power was then really lodged in the Crown, and because parliament met very seldom, and for other reasons, it was then necessary that, on a multitude of points, the Crown-should have much more power than is amply sufficient for it at present. But now the real power is not in the Sovereign, it is in the Prime Minister and in the cabinet-that is,, in the hands of a committee appointed by parliament, and of the chairman of that committee. Now, beforehand, no one would have-ventured to suggest that a committee of parliament on foreign relations should be able to-commit the country to the greatest international obligations without consulting either parliament or the country. No other select committee has any comparable power; and considering how carefully we have fettered and limited the powers of all other subordinate authorities, our allowing so much discretionary power on matters peculiarly dangerous and peculiarity delicate to rest in the sole charge of one secret committee is exceedingly strange. No doubt it may be beneficial; many seeming anomalies are so, but at first sight it does not look right.
Proceeding, be goes on to say:
It certainly would be in many ways advantageous to change it. If we require that in some the assent of parliament shall be given to such treaties, we should have a real dis-

ment would not be competent to give rise to any treaty whatsoever. The Earl, the Secretary of State, must at some time have been familiar with the debate between Mirabeau and Barnave, in the French Assembly, soon after 1789, as to where the power of making treaties should be vested. Mirabeau, on that point, an advocate of monarchy, contended that the power should be vested in the Sovereign. Barnave-the organ of the more popular idea -that it should be consigned to the Assembly. Mirabeau prevailed; the power resided in the Crown; but the veto of the legislative body was universally admitted-the initiative of the Crown and the veto of the legislative body were seen at once to be compatible. The prerogative would only suffer if treaties were allowed to emanate from any other origin. But it is just to go beyond that statement. When questions are irrevocably settled by negotiators at a blow, Sovereigns can have no voice in their conclusion.
Now, Sir, treaties of this kind aire made [DOT]purely by the negotiators, but these men are always ready to invoke the sovereign power, the royal prerogative, and while Ordinary every-day ministers making the [DOT]treaty they are always prepared to throw the cloak /of royalty around their shoulders *and tflius protect themselves from the con-csequences of their errors and failures.

When the House rose at six o'clock I was engaged in reading some remarks by Lord Campbell on the question whether treaties should be laid before parliament before they are ratified by the ambassadors. Unfortunately it is rather dull for the House to listen to extracts of this kind, but in order to support my argument I think it essential that these should

be placed upon ' Hansard/ as we may have occasion to discuss this matter again. I will now continue:
So long as they are forced to wait for parliamentary adhesion, a salutary influence may often be asserted by a Sovereign, informed on foreign policy and anxious for the honour of the country. By what goes on at present, courts and parliaments are simultaneously mocked. The last fear of scruple, it may be, perhaps, essential to remove, is connected with a view that flagrant innovation is demanded. Innovation as to detail there might be; but there would not, in point of fact, be any as to principle. The principle was long ago conceded. There is no class of treaties which it is more critical and delicate to expose to parliamentary discussion than those by which a war is ended. They give rise to passions the most various, and debates the most entangled. It may become necessary, with a view to justify the terms, to explain the decline of credit, the dissipation of resources, the misconduct of allies, the rottenness of vessels, and bring forward many other topics which prudence would avoid, and dignity, in some degree, recoil from. Much stronger argument may be advanced against parliamentary revision of treaties which lead to peace, than of those which pave the way for arbitration. But on treaties which conclude a war, since 1688, what has been the method usually adopted? As regards the first, that of Ryswick, the records are too scanty to determine. On that of Utrecht, which succeeds, materials are only too abundant. Lord Bolingbrooke, its celebrated author, has left undying pages on the subject. Preliminary articles were brought before both Houses, and so important was it deemed to gain the concurrence of this House that a dozen Peers were called into existence to secure it-this part of history can scarcely have escaped Her Majesty's government. The Peace of 1748 does not appear to have been conducted in this manner. Complaints were made in parliament about it. It was allowed to be the ignominious end of an unnecessary contest. The peace which followed the Seven Years' War in 1761-2, was brought with every possible solemnity before the Houses of that period. Lord Chatham, at that time Mr. Pitt, who had resigned, left a sick bed on purpose to oppose it. He took that course, it may be well supposed, not to execute a medical injunction, or to raise his credit as an orator, but, in the m'dst of pain and risk, to induce the House of Commons, if he could, to reject the preliminary articles. The Peace of 1783, which closed the struggle with America, was no less formally submitted to the legislature. Not only did debates occur-not only were they followed by divisions, but the government of Lord Shelburne was outvoted, and another set of public men required to negotiate. The beginning of the century was marked by the Peace of Amiens. Preliminary articles were brought before the Houses, against which Mr. Windham took the opportunity of delivering a speech, with which his face is, in a great degree, identified. The same process was repeated in 1814 and 1815. I am forced to hurry over it, that I may not exhaust the patience of the House. But the abilities of such men as Sir lames MacKintosh and Mr. Hormer
were brought to bear on criticism of the treaties before, not after they were sanctioned. In 1856, after the Crimean War, I readily admit that parliament was not consulted in that method, but that circumstance can hardly be accepted as an argument against the present motion. It merely indicates a tendency to overlook and to encroach on the authority which parliament enjoyed down to 1815, and which your Lordships are invited to restore as regards the class of treaties most in want of vigilant solicitude at present.
About the same time a motion was brought forward by Mr. Sinclair Aytoun in the House of Commons as follows:
In the opinion of this House, all treaties with foreign powers ought to be made conditionally on the approval of parliament, as was done in the case of the commercial treaty with France in 1860.
Mr._ Aytoun then proceeds to discuss the question, and asked what is the practice. I may say that this applies to this government now that this government has undertaken to make treaties, the line of action outlined in Mr. Aytoun's speech is the identical line followed, by our government here. Mr. Aytoun said:
What was the practice always followed by the government in making a treaty? No information was given to the House with regard to these treaty obligations until after they were settled. When a question was asked in the House, they were told that they should wait until the treaty was concluded, and then express their opinion as to the conduct of the government. In accordance with this practice, the Under Secretary for the Colonies declined, a session or so ago, to lay on the table a treaty with Holland before it had been ratified. Then, however, it was too late either to reject a treaty or to obtain any modification of its terms. He maintained that this practice was inconsistent with one of the well-ascertained rights of the people of this country. One of the best known provisions of the Bill of Rights was that all taxation by prerogative was illegal; and it followed that the practice which allowed the government to enter into engagements which would have the effect of imposing an immense amount of taxation on people must be unconstitutional. They were told that the House did maintain its control over foreign treaties, because the ministers were responsible to it; but cases might occur in which it would be impossible for the House to interfere until after a treaty was concluded and ratified. A government which had a large majority in parliament on a domestic question, might not be in harmony with the opinion of the country on questions of foreign policy. They had also had cases where a government did not actually possess a majority of the House; and it was, therefore, possible for a government not having a majority and not supported by the public, to enter into engagements during the recess of the gravest character. The safeguard of ministerial responsibility was perfectly illusory. They were told that the effect of such a change as that which he proposed would be

to take the conduct of foreign negotiations out of the hands of Her Majesty's government.
I might add in this connection a schedule of the treaties since that period. The following treaties between Great Britain and foreign powers since 1815, contained articles, the execution of which was [DOT]made contingent upon their confirmation by the British parliament:	On May 19,
1815, a treatv with Russia relating to payment of dividend of Russian-Dutch loan; November 17,	1823, a convention with
Austria about loan; November 16, 1831, a convention with Russia about Russian-Dutch loan-continuance of payment; May 7, 1832, the convention with France and Russia relating to Greek loan; August 2, 1839, a convention with France dealing with channel fisheries; May 28, 1852, a convention with France about extradition; January 25, 1855, convention with Sardinia about loan guarantee; June 27, 1855, convention with France and Turkey, relative to guarantee raised by the Sultan; June 3, 1855, a convention with Sardinia relating to loan; January 14, 1857, convention with France about Newfoundland fisheries; March 5, 1864, convention with Prussia relating to the subject of extradition; March 29, 1864, a treaty with France, Russia and Greece relating to Greek loan and pension to the King of the Hellenes; April 30, 1868, convention of Austria, Italy, Turkey, Prussia and France to guarantee loan to complete works on the Danube. There was no special article in the treaty of March 29, 1864, stating the sanction of parliament would be required for its execution, but an Act was passed for that purpose; and in the cases of the convention of May 28, 1852, the convention with France in January, 1857, and the convention with Russia in 1864, parliament exercised its powers and rejected the provisions which were submitted to it.
You will see that in all cases where there is involved a question of territory or war, or the guaranteeing of money, or anything in which taxation is involved in any shape, that very article is always inserted in the treaty, namely, that it requires the affirmation of parliament or parliamentary sanction. In this case we have no such articles, and I think with my hon. leader (Mr. Borden, Halifax), that this treaty, instead of being ratified by the Dominion parliament, should first be, ratified by the imperial parliament.
I cannot leave this subject without touching upon another one which, to my mind, is of very serious import. In the old country, in the mother of parliaments, the idea underlying treaty making is altogether different from that which underlies treaty making in any other country. For instance Great Britain has nothing to give in the way of trade privileges or rights, Mr. CURRIE (Simcoe).
and everything to obtain. Conseouently when she asks a treaty, she desires to get all the concessions possible whilst she has none to give, because of her free trade policy.
The idea underlying the principles of parliamentary government in the mother of parliaments, is that parliament does not represent the people; the people have the privilege of sending representatives to parliament, but the principle of representative government does not hold in Britain, and it is entirely an American idea. It is the principle on which the American revolution was fought, and I may say that it prevails in Canada, where we have fought elections on the principle of representative government. In view of the principle of representative government which prevails in Canada, the government of the day have violated that great principle when they sent ambassadors recently to Washington to bring about a trade treaty with the United States. Not only that, but the very men who violated that principle had the hardihood to come into this House and maintain that when they made that treaty they were invested with the royal prerogative and could pledge not only the honour of the cabinet but the honour of the country, and the honour of the British Crown to what they did. They told the House that not a line, or letter or figure in that treaty could be changed.	-
What treaty has the hon. gentleman reference to?

I am dealing with treaties generally, and I am pointing out that this government on every occasion it has taken part in treaty-making, especially with the United States, not only violated the principles of representative government, but betrayed the interests of the people.
I was wondering whether the hon. gentleman was referring to the recent trade agreement as a treaty, or whether he was speaking of something else.
What is the difference between a treaty and a convention?
If the hon. gentleman is referring to the recent trade agreement as a treaty, he is entirely mistaken, and he knows it.

The recent trade agreement is a treaty in every sense of the term. It was made subject to concurrent legislation; it was negotiated between representatives of both countries; the President of the United States signed it on behalf of the United States, and I say it is most shameful that this parliament should be wasting its time

	.

Mr. CURRIE (Simcoe)-Yes, wasting its time because the two ministers that were sent to Washington did not know anything about treaty-making, and they were humbugged by the President of the United States and buncoed into making a treaty which is no good and which they do not intend to put through, and which is making them the laughing stock of the whole country.
