speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman was- referring to the trade agreement and the matter of reciprocity as an illustratioin of the principle * of making treaties it was in order, but I would ask the hon. gentleman not to carry it further than that.

I am illustrating the manner in which the business of this country has been conducted by our treaty negotiators. In this treaty before us the Hon. Mr. Bryce was the negotiator, and the Minister of Public Works told us that he represented this country as its attorney. There has not been a single occasion when these treaties with the United States come up but what the fear was paramount in the mind of the Canadian negotiators, as one of them said this afternoon, that the United States was the dominant power on this continent. When did the United States become the dominant power on this continent? I tell these gentlemen opposite that the United States never was the dominant power on this continent, and that Great Britain has as many rights on this continent as the United States has.
The hon. gentleman who used that expression spoke of the dominant sovereignty of the United States in this matter.

The United States is not a sovereignty, but a republic, and they w-ould be the first to repudiate that they are a sovereignty. He said that the United States were the dominant power on this continent, and he said they could do anything they liked here, and he intimated that they could force an unjust principle upon us, and the leader of the House sat there and listened to him. If ever there was an example of members of the Canadian government holding a brief for a foreign country it was to be seen in the House this afternoon. The leader of the government sat silent when that statement was made, and he clearly showed the views of the members of this government that when they go into treaty making with the United States they go in with fear anti trembling, they think that Canada is only a
small, isolated power and that at any moment the United States can come in and capture this country the same as they are endeavouring to do with Mexico this very minute. I repudiate this idea. Canada is a part of the British Empire, and Britain has ever been ready to take part in her defence as occasion demanded. Great Britain is always ready to see that justice will be done between Canada and the United States or any other country. I said that when these two gentlemen went to Washington to make this trade treaty their knee3 were shaking under them. When they went down to Albany last spring, and the big stick was held up by the President of the United States, and he threatened the surtax against us, then it was that this Waterways Treaty was forced upon us, and that the rights of Canadian citizens were violated. I claim that this treaty is a violation of the rights of Canadians. Why should not the same just rule prevail as to water rights between two countries side by side, as would prevail as between two private individuals? But here we have gentlemen opposite rising in their seats tonight, evidently holding a brief for the United States in relation to every international question that comes up in this House, and asserting that we have to give away our rights in this matter. Objection was taken to the diversion of the waters of the Rainy river, and the minister interrupted, and' said that the commission refused to divert that water, but that the Secretary of War of the United States had given permission to divert all the waters on the American side flowing into the Rainy river, and keep them in American territory. There you have an example of what can be done by the United States. If firm ground had been taken by the Canadian government; if they placed their confidence in the mother country as they should have done, instead of continually endeavouring to break up the confederation of this country, as the leader of the government to-day in this House has done on every occasion, we would have less giving away of Canadian rights. Why, in a few years a Canadian dare not eat his breakfast unless^ he consults a joint international commission. Every sovereign right which Canada has on this continent will be invaded through the treaty making mania of hon. gentlemen opposite and especially the proxy premier who is the chief offender, and who leads the House to-night.
He is the leading man in trying to get the United States to edge into our affairs. We have a joint commission on waterways, and a joint commission on fisheries; we shall soon have a joint commission on railways. The next thing will be a joint commission on farming, and no one will be able to grow wheat in the Northwest

unless he gets the permission of that joint commission. For the first time in a British country, a foreign country has been allowed to interfere with our rights of taxation. Pitt laid down the principle that if you allow a foreign parliament to interfere with your rights of taxation you have allowed it to enter the citadel, and all hope of' your country is gone. We have allowed the United States to dictate to us in matters of taxation, and we are allowing it to dictate to us in regard to our water-powers. The Niagara river is dealt with here. At one time the only thing about the Niagara Falls was the scenery and some land, and when a division was made under the old treaty, the United States took all they could take, which was the land. They took all the islands in the river that were worth anything, and they left to us the Horseshoe Fall, which they did not think was valuable; but just as the water becomes valuable, we find them seeking to put this treaty through so that they will get more than their fair share of the water. The House will understand that the Niagara Falls were surveyed by their surveyor, named Hunter, and -then they had the gall to come to this commission and say, we have not been able to find that old survey, so we will make a new survey, and we will try to divide the water equally so that we will get more of it than we have now. They first got the islands and the land, and now they want the water as well. You find them acting in the same way in regard to everything. The Americans have never made a treaty with any country that they have kept unless it has been to their advantage. Where did the name reciprocity first occur? They made a treaty with France in the early part of the last century with reference to trading rights in Louisiana, and no sooner had they made it than they tried to hedge and not carry out its provisions. Take the Bulwer-Clayton treaty with regard to ships on the lakes-they are not keeping that. Another treaty said that they could not fortify the Panama canal, and they are not keeping that, but are going to fortify the canal. As a man of war I am a great believer in peace. Every one who knows anything about war must recognize its terrible horrors. None of the gentlemen have ever encountered war or seen anything of its horrors. But, whenever I see any country beginning to preach peace, I have a very strong idea that before long that country is going to be engaged in a great war. Who was the first and principal mover in founding the peace establishment at the Hague? The Czar of Bussia; and inside of a year he was involved in the greatest and most sanguinary war in the history of the world-the war with Japan.

I risq to a point of order, but before stating the point, I would like to know whether it would be easier to let the hon. gentleman go on or to stop him. I think he should come down to a discussion of this Bill. Our time is precious, we are approaching the time when we want to adjourn, and the hon. gentleman will surely see the propriety of discussing the merits of this Bill.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The section before the House is to confirm a certain treaty which is in the schedule. I think the hon. gentleman's remarks, while very broad, are entirely, along the line of the treaty and treaty-making, and I have not felt that he has transgressed'the rule.

Of course, this is not a matter that the Minister of Public Works likes to have any reference made to; but I was referring to the subject of peace in order to point out that the United States at the present moment, while talking of a peace treaty with every other country, has a large army on the borders of Mexico ready to jump the line on ten minutes'-notice; and I have no hesitation in saying that if the circumstances do not change in the next few months, there will be a great war between the United States and Mexico, perhaps the greatest war that has ever taken place on this continent. Hon. gentlemen opposite, in making their treaty, have shown themselves afraid of the United States, the dominant power. They know that the United States can take all these water-powers from them. They have gone down on their knees on every occasion when they have had a treaty to make with that country. On every occasion that they have had anything to give away to the United States, they have given it away. If they go on making treaties very much longer, we shall not have any of this country left. Some fine morning we may be told that negotiators have gone to Washington, and have turned over Canada or some of its provinces to the United States, and according to the principle laid down by the government of the day, they have a right to do that, and then come down to this House and say, we have made this treaty, we have given away Alberta and Saskatchewan and Manitoba to the United States, and you have no right to question that, because your ambassadors have pledged the honour of the country that that should be done, and this parliament of Canada has no right to change a letter in that agreement; the only thing it can do is put the government out of office. Carrying out what I said in my opening remarks, I think that before any treaty or bargain of any kind is made with the United States, preliminary articles relative to what is intended to be done should be

laid on the table of this House, so that the members of this parliament could discuss them, and give the government of the day the advantage of the knowledge of how it will affect the various constituencies represented here, in order that when the treaty is made, it can be brought to this House, and there will be no objection or opposition to it. I claim that in the pact recently made this country has been betrayed again and again in that respect. Parliament has been made the laughing stock .of this whole country. We are kept here for months discussing a treaty of which there is no possible solution. It is a bargain which the Americans, judging by the action of their Senate, have no apparent intention of carrying through. If this government desired to act in a dignified manner, they would have told the United States government that before this country proceeded with any treaty of that character it would be necessary for Congress first to adopt it. We have a precedent in this very treaty, which the United States Congress has already passed before it is submitted to us. For that reason I think this tariff treaty should be dealt with in a similar manner.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I think the hon. gentleman is now referring to the tariff treaty in a manner not warranted by the circumstances. He may draw an illustration from the tariff arrangement and apply it to this section, but I think he is now reversing that.

I have no intention to transgress the rules, but I wish merely to point out that this treaty, which we are now asked to pass, was passed by the United States Senate and Congress, as will be seen on page 11 of the Bill:
The above treaty was approved by the United States Senate on the 3rd March, 1909, with the following resolution:	_
Resolved, that the Senate advise and consent to the ratification of the treaty between the United States and Great Britain, providing for the settlement of international differences between the United States and Canada, signed on the 11th day of January, 1909.
I claim that that should have been taken as a precedent, and that this House should not have wasted' three or four months uselessly discussing a reciprocity treaty which I do not think the United States have any intention of passing. Whenever we go to make any treaties with the United States again, I would suggest that this procedure be followed. If the government desires to maintain its dignity, and the honour of this country, it should proceed at once to withdraw this proposed reciprocity treaty, and follow the procedure given in this Bill.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is again using an argument which
I ruled out of order. He has no right to discuss the reciprocity pact on this measure.

Then I shall reverse the argument and say that we are wrong in carrying out this treaty now, that it should not be brought before the House in this manner, but that it should have been passed by this House before it was submitted to the United States Congress. That shows the absurdity of the whole thing. This House, and the whole of Canada has been made a laughing stock by the United States government in order to advance the interests of a vote-seeking President, and a political party whose cause seems to be pretty nearly lost.

I was very much surprised when this Bill was presented by the hon. the Minister of Pubic Works (Mr. Pugsley). I see him smiling. I suppose he has changed his mind.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Will my hon. friend be good enough to quote the passage.
I shall look it up in a few minutes. The Minister of Finance has a bad memory sometimes when it suits him. Who made this treaty?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman can have all the information he can desire about this treaty from my hon. colleague the Minister of Public Works.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Minister of Finance takes a different view.

It is rather strange that the moment we ask for any information from the Minister of Finance, who is leading the House, he gets wrathy. I ask him who made this treaty? Surely some Canadian representative made it? Was it the hon. minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Minister of Public Works is dealiing with this treaty and will be very happy to answer any questions of a proper character.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He thinks differently.
Why does my hon. friend not want to ask me?

I have no objection since the Minister of Finance will not

reply. I would like to know what minister of the government had charge of this treaty when it was being negotiated at Washington.

The interests of the Canadian government were looked after by Mr. Gibbons, the chairman of the International Waterways Commission, who was constantly in conference with the Britisli ambassador, and who was assisted by Dr. King and Mr. Campbell, both of the Department of the Interior. On different occasions I went to Washington to render w'hat assistance I could, and the Minister of Justice (Sir Allen Aylesworth) also went to render assistance at one stage in the negotiations.

I want to understand what took place.
I have stated exactly what took place.

As I understand it, the Minister of Public Works and the Minister of Justice are really the two government representatives who had charge of this Bill at Washington. There must have been some one to assume the responsibility because the International Waterways Commission surely would not have the power to negotiate a treaty. If thev did negotiate it up to a certain point, the Minister of Public Works and the Minister of Justice assumed the responsibility. Am I right?
I have stated exactly what took place.
I think that the attitude of these two gentlemen is most unfair; and if they want this Bill to go through they will have to change their tactics.

How could I make the matter plainer? I stated who negotiated the treaty, I made reference to the services of the British ambassador in that connection, I stated the part the Minister of Justice and I performed. That is all the information I can give my hon. friend, and on reflection he will see that is all he could ask me to give. I intended no discourtesy, but answered fullv and frankly.
Did the government as a whole delegate the Minister of Public Works and the Minister of Justice to negotiate this treaty?

The Minister of Justice, when he went to Washington, and I, when Mr. REID (Grenville)
I went there, went with the authority of the government.

Then the negotiation of this treatv was practically delegated to the Minister of Public Works and the Minister of Justice on behalf of Canada, and they are responsible for the treaty being in its present shape.
The whole government is responsible.

The government assumed the work done by these two gentlemen. What I was trying to find out was whether this treaty, as it now stands, is in the same form as was arranged between the Minister of Public Works and the Minister of Justice on behalf of the Canadian government. Will the Minister of Public Works reply?

I do not think I can give my hon. friend any more information.
Mr. REID (Grenville) What I am surprised at is this: This Bill has been before the House some time. I think the original Bill was Bill (No. 36) with only three clauses in it, and at that time the point was raised as to whether the commission would have power to decide certain questions regarding water-powers on the St. Lawrence. There was also a question as to the ratification of this treaty by parliament. The ground was then taken that the treaty did not require to be ratified by this parliament; yet to-day, just when the minister wishes to pass this Bill, down it comes m a different shape altogether. There are men not now in this House who were here a few days ago and very anxious about this Bill, but they took _ it for granted that the Bill submitted originally was the only one that would come before this House. They have no opportunity of studying this Bill, and the effect of the changes that have been made in it. This is practically a new Bill, and the government ought not to ask this parliament to ratify it without giving the members an opportunity of seeing what effect these changes will have. I think the Minister of Public Works took the ground that the United States, if they wished, could divert a stream through thfeir own territory into another channel altogether, and we could not interfere.
Always excepting any diversion which would interfere with the navigability of a river.
Take the point at the Long Sault rapids, what effect would it have, supposing they dammed the St. Lawrence river on American territory?

I may say that this treaty would give no authority whatever to dam the St. Lawrence at the Long Sault

or anywhere else. The words of this treaty are simply prohibitory, they are not permissive; and in addition to 'getting the authority of this parliament to construct a dam in the river, the plans would also have to be approved by the Boundary Waters Commission. It does not take away the necessity of first obtaining the authority of parliament.

On the American side they take a different view. The Bill was up in Congress during the last session when the representative of the New York legislature claimed that the New York legislature had the right to dam the St. Lawrence. The House of Representatives passed the Bill, and if it had not been so late in the session the chances are that the Senate would have passed' it too. Now what confidence can we have that the United States government will keep faith with Canada in regard to this treaty? If the Bill had passed, how could we have prevented them going on and building the dam on the St. Lawrence? There would have been a Bill passed by the New York legislature, who own the bed of the river and they would have got the Washington Congress to pass a Bill of the same nature. If they had started to build that dam we could not have prevented it unless we had gone to war. Now, what confidence can we have that Washington will keep faith when we make treaties with them? As my hon. friend from Simcoe (Mr. Currie), has shown, they have violated treaties in other cases. As I mentioned the other night, they have violated a treaty in placing war vessels on the Great Lakes, and when there was trouble they simply got the consent of the State government to allow them to go through the canals. This government never objected. During all these years the United States have compelled vessels going from Ottawa to New York to unload on the frontier, while vessels from New York could come right straight through to Ottawa. But as soon as this reciprocity agreement came up, and the fisheries treaty, and the waterways treaty, then the United States government allowed these vessels to go through the canals. I mention these facts to show that the United States government have not in the past kept good faith with us. Now, this treaty, when it is passed, will be entirely in their favour, and Canada will get the worst of it.
In what respect is it in their favour?
Why, it is in their favour if they can dam the St. Lawrence.
There is a big 'if' in your suggestion.
The Minister of Public Works was the first man to give it to them.
No, he was not.

The Minister of Public Works stated in this House,that he was considering it, and that he would protect Canada's interest by charging some rate, and that the New York State government was to charge $35,000 per annum.
I said nothing of the kind.
The Minister of Public Works knows he did refer to the way he was safe-guarding Canada's interests.
He did not state at all what the hon. gentleman has just said.

The Minister of Public Works was considering the advisability of letting this great work go through. Why is the Minister of Public Works so awfully anxious to protect navigation from the Long Sault rapids? The whole navigation east of that is in Canada, there is no part of the St. Lawrence river on the American side from the Long Sault rapids down, it is all in Canada. Now if this treaty goes through, it only requires one of our Canadian commissioners to agree with three American commissioners in order to carry through any proposition that is made in these great waters between Canada and the United States. I have consulted lawyers on this question, and they differ from the Minister of Public Works.
They say they believe that, if this treaty goes through, this International Waterways Commission will have the right to decide. All I want to do is to protect Canadian interests so that they will be beyond dispute. Let us see the position we should be in if they assumed the right and this work went on. In the first place, if a dam were built at the Long Sault rapids, these commissioners agreeing to it, the private corporation would have absolute control of that great work. They build locks there. It is true, they are willing to put in a Bill that the government can control these locks. But then the United States government and the Canadian government jointly control them. If trouble should arise between Canada and the United States, or between Great Britain and the United States, the treaty comes to an end, and, as the locks are on the American side of the river we should not have the control of the navigation that we now have. Or if the dam should break or anything of that kind occur, our canal system would not be in proper shape to take vessels through, because the effect of damming the St. Law-



rence would be to raise the water at the head of the Cornwall canal and so our canal system would have to be changed to meet the new conditions. I object to this work going on at the Long Sault rapids because I believe it is going to divert tradfe to American seaports. For instance, you place the foot of navigation for the Americans down at the Long Sault or at Massena. The distance to Portland is not very great, so that grain trade and other trade could be diverted from Montreal. Again, I object to the whole water-power that might be developed there getting into the hands of a private corporation and practically into the United States. For vested interests will arise, and once these privileges have been given we cannot possibly destroy them. If this treaty were sufficiently protected, if nothing could be done there without this parliament having to agree to it-that is so far as placing any obstruction or dam across the St. Lawrence or alter it in any way-it would certainly remove my objection to the treaty to a very great extent.

I may say to my hon. friend, he may not take my word for it- that it is made absolutely clear by the treaty that it must be by consent of the Dominion of Canada, and that means the parliament of Canada. Read article 3.

That is the one I had in mind:
It is agreed that, in addition to the uses, obstructions, and diversions heretofore permitted or hereafter provided for by special agreement between the parties hereto, no further or other uses or obstructions or diver-sit ns, whether temporary or permanent, of boundary waters on either side of the line, affecting the natural flow level or flow of boundary waters on the other side of the line, shall be made except by authority of the United States or the Dominion of Canada within their respective jurisdictions and with the approval, as hereinafter provided, of a joint commission, to be known as the International Joint Commission.
So, you must have the double approval, first of the Dominion of Canada and then of the commission.
I have had two or three leading lawyers examine that clause, and they tell me that it might be construed directly opposite to what the Minister of Public Works says.
How did they say it might be construed?
That the commission could decide that.
But does it not say: * The Dominion of Canada '? That does not mean the commission. It adds ' and the commission.'
It does not say that the sanction shall be of this parliament, but of the Dominion of Canada, and this commission that we are appointing will represent the Dominion of Canada.
Oh, no.

In other words, it will represent the minister. Certainly I would like to see the clause a little plainer. My attention is called to this clause which reads:	' Shall not be made except by the
authorities of the United States or the Dominion of Canada.' The minister said we would have to have the consent of the United States, and the Dominion o>f Canada. But it says ' or,' and not ' and.'
'Within their respective jurisdictions.'
But this is practically all in the United States. If you have the consent of one or the other

If my hon. friend will pardon me I may be able to make clear my own view. I think it is absolutely clear that the United States cannot do anything which will alter the actual level or flow of boundary waters on the Canadian side except with the authority of the Dominion of Canada, and the approval of the Joint Commission; and Canada can do nothing to alter the actual level or flow of boundary waters on the United States side without the consent of the United States, and of the commission also. So that, so far as the countries are concerned, you must have the two things-you must have the consent of that country and you must have the approval of the Joint Commission.

I will have to leave that to be argued by some person who is better qualified than I am, or by some lawyer who would understand the cause better, but I have heard it argued by lawyers who express a different opinion from that of the Minister of Public Works and who claim that the clause is not clear and that if the Joint Commission did agree to this it would be impossible for us to dispute it. If the minister wishes this to be thoroughly understood, to protect the rights of Canada, and to carry out the promise made by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Public Works himself that they would guarantee that this work would not be carried out without first coming to parliament, then I \yould suggest that he put in another clause
What is that?

Something like this:
Nothing in this Act nor in the appointment of the commissioners to be appointed by His Majesty pursuant to the said treaty and under

this Act shall empower or he interpreted as empowering the commissioners so to be appointed, or the said commission to assent to authorize or approve of the erection or maintenance of any dams, locks or other obstructions in any or all of the channels of the St. Lawrence rh er mentioned in section 7 of the treaty made between Great Britain and the United States, dated August 9, A.D. 1842, upon either side of the boundary line for any purpose whatsoever, nor shall the said commissioners or said commission be empowered to pass upon or determine nor pass upon or determine the question as to whether or not any proposed dams or locks or other obstructions at said place will or will not either impair or improve navigation.
The minister can see the object of that section.

I regret that I cannot
see it in face of the express words of the treaty.

This would be a clause in this Bill. It does not alter the treaty but it expressly tells the commission that in so far as that clause in the Ashburton treaty is concerned, there shall be no misunderstanding between this parliament and these men that we are now appointing. We cannot change the treaty here without going back to Washington. They would have to agree to any change that is made in the wording of the treaty, but this would place beyond doubt what the wishes of parliament are if such a case should come before the commission. Where you find a difference of opinion between leading lawyers in Canada, in so far as the construction which can be placed upon clause 3 is concerned, I cannot see why the Minister of Public Works should object to something being placed in the Bill on the lines I suggest in order to keep this matter perfectly right, and in order that the promise that the Prime Minister and the Minister of Public Works made to this House should be carried out. This question may not come up before the commission within a few months, or if, at any future time, there was a change in the positions of the gentlemen who have given us this promise, this project might go through and we could have no recourse. At all events, I cannot see whv the Minister of Public Works should object to placing this parliament in a position that there can be no possible chance of a misunderstanding of that kind occurring. This great work at the Long Sault rapids is not being done for the improvement of navigation. That issue was raised at Washington and those who are proposing this work state that water-power is the first consideration, not navigation. That being the case, why should we interfere with navigation or place it in a secondary position? There is no doubt that the trip down the St. Lawrence and through the rapids is a very 2901
important part of our navigation system.. It attracts a gr6at many persons, we liku to see them and it advertises Canada. la so far as it being necessary to furnish power for the frontier is concerned, I may say that has been taken up by the Hydro-Electric Commission and, as I understand, they, are offering a very cheap rate for power along the frontier. Therefore, I think that the objection from the frontier is being-overcome.
Does my hon. friend1 know where they are going to get the-power?

I understood from; the minister who has charge of the Power-Commission that there are two, I think three sources. There is one power company that, I think, could supply Kingston at any time and they are trying to negotiate with them now. That is the Seymour Power Company of Trenton. I think that-they would come down further if there was a sufficient consumption of power to guarantee the enterprise. There is another large power about to be developed at a place called Calabogie back of Kingston.
I have seen something in the papers about getting power from Waddington.
There is that source too.	*
What would be the effect on the canals of the development of power there?
None whatever. It would not affect the river at all.

The hon. member from Dundas (Mr. Broder) asked me two or three weeks ago to lay on the table of the House a report which had been ordered some-weeks before with regard to this matter. In my absence it was laid on the table of the House, and I have only had an opportunity of casually looking it over, but the opinion seemed to be very strong that it would affect the Morrisburg canal very-much if they developed as much power there as they are talking about.
Of course, the Minister of Railways and Canals knows-that section well. The only way it could affect it, I suppose, would be that it would1 make more water.

It would increase the discharge and draw more water away from>
the other part of the river.
I would like to-know how it could affect it.
I remember discussing this question with the engineer. He calculates that it would reduce the water on the sill at the head of the Morrisburg canal'

*one inch for every thousand horse-power developed at Waddington. It is a low head and they would have to make their dams in a way that would draw off a great volume of water from the main channel into the little river in order to develop power and this would decrease the depth on the sili. I do not know anything about it person-[DOT]ally.
Who is the principal *owner of the power at Waddington?
Mr. Allison.
He is the gentleman who appeared in New York in opposition 'to the other one?

He is the gentle-*man who appeared in New York. I was under the impression it would raise the water at the head of the canal because it would dam it back. However, I am not going to argue against the engineer.
Look at the report; I do mot know anything about it personally.
But it strikes me that it would have a very decided effect. That being so, if the dam were built at the Long Sault rapids it would take the water away from the Cornwall canal altogether.
It depends altogether *on your flume and upon the depth to which you can draw the water.

If it acts that way at Waddington it will have the same effect at the Cornwall canal and draw the water from the head of that canal, and our canal system at Cornwall, on which we spent so much money, will be spoiled. We can now run a steamer from Kingston to Montreal altogether in Canadian waters, but if these locks are built we will be going through the American lock, and while there is no objection to that so long as everything is all right, yet you cannot tell when something will happen, and then there will be trouble. I urge strongly that the consent of parliament shall be obtained before anything is done in this matter.
That is the law now; no such plan can be approved without the authority of parliament.
When other gentlemen of high legal repute give an opinion to the contrary, is it not well to make it sure?
What legal gentleman has given a contrary opinion?

I do not wish to mention names, but there are able lawyers in Canada who hold that the clause is not clear, and that if the commission decided to place a dam there it would be difficult Mr. GRAHAM.
for the government to interfere. I do not belittle the opinion of the Minister of Justice or the Minister of Public Works, but lawyers, like doctors, differ. What objection can there be to the clause I suggest?
Will the hon. gentleman send it over to me?

If the opinion of the Minister of Public Works is right, the insertion of this clause can do no harm, and it will remove any doubt there may arise in the mind of the commission. The promoters of this great scheme will no doubt be back here for legislation, and it is this parliament which should decide whether they will proceed with the work or not. This clause simply gives effect to the understanding announced by the Prime Minister and by the Minister of Public Works in this House.
I would like to oblige my hon. friend, but I would not like to put ourselves on record as doing a very foolish and very unnecessary thing.
You do that often.
The less we do of it the better.
You do it so often that really it does not make much difference.

The clause my hon. friend wants inserted is as follows:
Nothing in this Act nor in the appointment of the commissioners to be appointed by His Majesty pursuant to the said treaty and under this Act shall empower or be interpreted as empowering the commissioners so to be appointed, or the said commission to assent to authorize or approve of the erection or maintenance of any dams, locks or other obstructions in any or all of the channels of the St. Lawrence river mentioned in section 7 of the treaty made between Great Britain and the United States, dated August 9, A.D. 1842, upon either side of the boundary line for any purpose whatsoever, nor shall the said commissioners or said commission be empowered to pass upon or determine nor pass upon or determine the question as to whether or not any proposed dams or locks or other obstructions at said place will or will not either impair or improve navigation.
If the latter part of that clause were adopted the commissioners would be absolutely powerless to approve or disapprove even if parliament had granted the necessary authority to erect any works in boundary water. Anyway the clause is entirely unnecessary because at last session of parliament, to make assurance doubly sure, even after the Prime Minister had made the statement that the government would not consent to any plans for the obstruction of the St. Lawrence river by erecting a dam

therein without first having the approval of parliament, section 12, chapter 166, 1910, was enacted.

That is exclusively
with regard to the authorizing of works upon our side of the river. It has nothing to do with works upon the American side.
Quite so. As to works on the American side of the river, we have, of course, no authority outside of the authority given by this treaty, and in this treaty is the safeguard.
What in the opinion of the hon. minister is the safeguard?

So far as Canada is concerned, we have the absolute provision that no works by way of dams, or other obstructions shall be erected in the St. Lawrence without the plans being first submitted to, and approved of by parliament. As to anything that may be done on the American side of the line, as it might affect the rights of the other country, article 3 provides:
It is agreed that, in addition to the uses, obstructions, and diversions heretofore permitted or hereafter provided for hy special agreement between the parties hereto, no further or other uses or obstructions or diversions, whether temporary or permanent, of boundary waters on either side of the line, affecting the natural level or flow of boundary waters on the other side of the line, shall be made except by authority of the United States or the Dominion of Canada within their respective jurisdictions and with the approval, as hereinafter provided, of a joint commission, to be known as the International Joint Commission.
I cannot conceive of language which would be more prohibitory than that. In other words, these two countries agree that there shall be no obstructions of any kind or description placed in these boundary waters which will affect the natural level, or flow of the water upon the other side of the line without the consent of the country in which such natural level or flow would be affected, or without the approval of this International Joint Commission. Under these circumstances, I could not ask the committee, with any reason, to accept the amendment which my hon. friend proposes It is not necessary, as all interests are safeguarded by the treaty.

I think there can be no two opinions as to the meaning of article 3. The effect of it and of the whole treaty, as I interpret it, is this. The boundary waters are waters in common. The waters that flow on the American side of the boundary line are in American territory, and those that flow on the Canadian side are in Canadian territory. Each party has an easement in the waters of the other for the treaty
purposes. What article 3 says is simply this: no uses, obstructions or diversions of water shall take place on either side of the river without the consent, first, of the country in which such uses, obstructions or diversions are to be created, or without also the consent of the commission. According to the minister's interpretation, it would not be necessary to get the consent of the country in which the use or obstruction or diversion takes place.

Article 3 proceeds on the theory that each country, so far as its own territory is concerned, can legislate, but it also expressly provides that neither country shall authorize the construction of works in its territory which would alter the flow or level of the water in the adjoining country without the consent of that country, or without the consent also of the International Joint Commission. That is clear. He who runs may read and understand that and there cannot be any doubt.

It is quite obvious that article (3) does not require the consent of both countries, the consent of one is sufficient provided the commission also gives its consent. Suppose an .obstruction be created on the American side
It must be a work authorized by that country.
Then the consent of that country is the only consent needed, since article (3) only requires the consent of one country.
You get the consent of the country in which the water level is being altered.

You must have the authority of the United States or of the Dominion of Canada and the consent of the commission, so that if the minister be right, the consent of the country on whose side the obstruction is to be created would not require to be secured. That is obviously absurd. There is no provision requiring the consent of both countries. If the minister be right in saying that you must have the consent of the country on whose side the water is raised, you do not require the consent of the country on whose side the.-obstruction is being created.

There is absolutely no doubt that the interpretation of my hon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Macdonell) is the only one possible of this section. I feel perfectly warranted in saying this because I can cite the express declaration of a lawyer for whose opinion, I am sure, the Minister of Public Works will have much greater respect than he can possibly haver
*^195

for mine or that of my hon. friend, I refer ' to the Minister of Justice. On the 2nd of February, page 2970, the Minister of Justice said:
Surely both can well stand together, the Ashburton treaty securing equal freedom for purposes of navigation-that is, freedom equally do the inhabitants of one country and those of :the other country-in the river which constitutes the boundary, and the recent treaty providing that no new obstruction shall be put anywhere along that river on either side of the line which will have the effect of raising the level on the other side of the line, except: *First, with the authority of the government [DOT] of the country in which the obstruction is to be placed, and, second, with the approval of "the International Joint Commission. Now, that language, I say, implies that the government of each country has the right to authorize, if it sees fit, such an obstruction as will alter the level on the other side of the line, and that obstruction, when it has been authorized by the proper government, must also receive the approval of the International Joint Commission before it can be permitted -the two things must concur. The language implies that there is a right, without any infraction of treaty obligations, on the part of either Canada or the United State9 to authorize such obstruction as may affect the level on the other side of the boundary if, in the judgment of the legislature of Canada or the United States, such obstruction is desirable. Now, we have a proposition in the Congress of the United States to authorize such an obstruction. It is entirely within their legal right; they are not infringing upon any treaty obligation by entertaining that proposition. But, if they see fit to authorize it, then, if it will affect the level on the Canadian side of the boundary, it must receive the approval of the International Joint Commission before it can be permitted. That is an additional safeguard which we have secured by entering into this recent treaty.
I asked the Minister of Public Works [DOT]what was the safeguard which the treaty gave us, and I understood him to say our safeguard was that our parliament had to authorize the creation of an obstruction on the American side. Evidently he and the Minister of Justice do not agree. The only safeguard we can have is that which the treaty gives us, and I do not think it gives us that which the Minister of Public Works says it does. The only safeguard it does give, in cases where it does apply, is the [DOT]consent of the International Commission *which must be obtained after the country on whose side the obstruction is created authorizes that obstruction. So that the country on whose side the level of the water is altered by the obstruction created on the opposite side has no voice in the matter but has to depend on the ruling of the Joint Commission. If anything more is wanted than the words of the first paragraph of the section, we need only read the second paragraph which makes it clear that if there be no interference with the Mr. DOHERTY.	,
flow of water on the other side, either country may go on and construct whatever works it thinks necessary for the improvement of navigation or other purposes mentioned in that section without the consent of the commission. The Joint Commission therefore has only warrant to interfere in cases when the obstruction created on the one side alters the level of the water on the other. But there is absolutely nothing to entitle the parliament of Canada to be consulted and required to authorize works to be built on the American side. The wording of the section leaves no possible doubt:
It is agreed that, in addition to the uses, obstructions, and diversions heretofore permitted or hereafter provided for by special agreement between the parties hereto, no further or other uses or obstructions or diversions, whether temporary or permanent, of boundary waters on either side of the line, affecting the natural level or flow of boundary waters on the other side of the line, shall be made except by authority of the United States or the Dominion of Canada within their respective jurisdictions.
That is to say, if you are going to make any use or obstruction, the United States must authorize those that are made within its jurisdiction and Canada must authorize those that are made within its jurisdiction. That is, the agreement of the United States with Canada is that it shall be made by the United States and not by the state of New York or any other authority. We undertake on our side that nothing shall be done by any authority other than that of the Dominion of Canada. And the protection of either party so far as the level of the water is concerned, is in the Joint Commission. But, if there be any possible doubt as to what the first paragraph means, the second paragraph makes it absolutely clear:
The foregoing provisions are not intended to limit or interfere with the existing rights of the government of the United States, on the one side, and the government of the Dominion of Canada, on the other, to undertake and carry on governmental works in boundary waters for the deepening of channels, the construction of breakwaters, the improvement of harbours, and other governmental works for the benefit of commerce and navigation, provided that such works are wholly on its own side of the line and do not materially affect the level or flow of the boundary waters on the other, nor are such provisions intended to interfere with the ordinary use of such waters for domestic and sanitary purposes.
It seems to me that makes it absolutely clear that, as regards this question of damming the "channels at the Long Sault, in the first place it is absolutely untenable to say that that clause has one word which requires authorization by this parliament of constructions in any of these portions of the channels that are on the American side- and the two channels which are governed

by the Ashburton treaty are practically entirely on the American side;-and, in the second place, that it is absolutely untenable to say that this Waterways Commission has one word to say about it unless the level of the water on our side is affected, but that if that water could be dammed in these two channels and these two channels blocked without altering the level of the water on the Canadian side, not even the commission would have a word to say about it, and, so far as this treaty is concerned, the American government might do just as it pleased. But, as I understand him, tlje hon. minister contends that this treaty requires both the assent of our parliament and the assent of the Waterways Commission, and provides that with these two things this damming operation could be carried on lawfully by the United States. It seems to me that, even if that interpretation be erroneous, as I think with all due respect it is in so far as attributing any right in our parliament to speak in opposition to doing that, and even if it be not sound to say that in that case apart from the question of affecting the level of the water, the consent of the Waterways Commission would be required, and, being given, would be sufficient,-yet because that interpretation is put upon it, it behooves this parliament which is called upon to ratify this treaty, to say whether or not it is willing to enact the legislation without repudiating that interpretation-Now I understand, the minister says, that the enactment of this amendment may be a useless and foolish thing. There might be a great deal of force in that if the minister were not asking us if that interpretation be clearly right or clearly wrong to do the useless and foolish thing of ratifying the treaty, over which we have no power. The treaty is in force, and has been in force for two years, as the Minister of Justice told us; and yet parliament is seriously sitting here to-night to ratify, sanction and approve it. It seems to me that that is at least as foolish and useless a thing as putting in this proviso, which is only useless and foolish if it has no effect. Now, to my mind, this treaty does not give to the Waterways Commission, which is created under it, any powers whatever to consent to the damming of these two channels. The government which is presenting this Bill to us tells us that it does, and we are asked to ratify and confirm it.

Surely my hon. friend is in error. I never made such a statement, that the treaty gives the commission power to authorize the obstruction of the river. I said it must be by the ' authority of parliament and the commission.

If the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) should happen to be wrong and the Minister of Justice (Sir
Allen Aylesworth) should happen to be right

If the hon. member will pardon me: The minister and my hon. friend (Mr. Doherty) both, I think, agree that, at all events, so far as the Canadian side is concerned as to any obstructions being placed in the river, that must be with the consent of parliament.
Undoubtedly. But we are not in danger, at present at all events, of obstruction on our side of the river. That is not the question which presents itself.
That is the question brought up by the member for Grenville (Mr. Reid).

I understood that hon. member to say that what he was anxious about was the proposed damming of the two channels referred to in the Ashburton treaty; and the amendment makes that dear, because it nrovides that nothing in this Act or in the appointment of these men, shall be interpreted as affecting the rights of Canada under the Ashburton Treaty.', The rights of Canada under the Ashburton Treaty are rights in channels on the American side-we do not need the Ashburton treaty to give us rights on our own side. What we want to preserve is the rights, such as they may be, which we have in these two channels, and what the hon. member for Grenville (Mr. Reid) seeks to do by his amendment is to make it absolutely clear, that, at all events so far as this legislation is concerned, it is not intended to modify those rights nor affect them in any way. Now, one of two things is true: Either this new waterways treaty has wiped out our rights under the Ashburton treaty and substituted these provisions for the Ashburton treaty, or it has not produced that effect. If it does produce that effect, and if under this treaty the assent of the commission is sufficient to authorize and make binding on Canada works constructed by the authority of the American government in these channels, of course we cannot alter the situation, and the amendment of the hon. member for Grenville does not undertake to alter that. But what it undertakes to do is to provide that this legislation which we are passing now, shall not alter that situation.
Now, I think, in view of the interpretation put upon the treaty by the minister, of Justice the desirability of that amendment becomes perfectly clear, unless parliament wishes by this legislation to enact that the commission should have power to bind Canada, by recognizing the right of the American government to authorize the blocking of these two channels, so far as they are in American waters, and they are practically

altogether in American waters. The purpose of the amendment is to guard against the effect being attributed to our ratification of this treaty, and our ratification of this treaty coming on top of the opinion of the Minister of Justice, that under this treaty the proposed damming of these two channel's, if assented to by this Waterways Commission, would be binding on Canada, It is to guard ourselves against the effect of such ah interpretation as given by the Minister of Justice. We have ratified the treaty but we do not intend that this ratification should be invoked in support of the contention that that is a proper interpretation, and that these commissioners have this authority. The purpose of the amendment is to make perfectly clear that the power of the commissioners should be just exactly what it would be under the treaty, but nothing additional should come to them by reason of the enactment of this statute. It is a measure of precaution. But at the same time, the interpretation that has been put upon the treaty, and our proceeding in face of that interpretation, without a word of explanation, t'o ratify it, would put a strong argument in the mouth of those who would have an interest in urging that by this legislation, and by the appointment of the commissioners to be made under it, we were confiding to them in toto all the voice that Canada may ever have with regard to damming these two channels. If the interpretation of the minister should happen to be wrong, the amendment will at least serve this purpose, it will make clear that parliament, in enacting this ratification, does not intend to adopt the opinion of the Minister of Justice and give it statutory effect, and is not handing over this particular matter to this commission, and giving them the whole power to speak for Canada. If the opinion of the Minister of Justice be the correct interpretation, notwithstanding that amendment to the statute, these gentlemen will have that power under the treaty. For my part it does not seem to me that the treaty itself gives to these gentlemen of the commission any power to deal with the question of the obstruction of these two channels. The purpose of the control that is given to these gentlemen is to put them in a position to prevent works on one side of the river which raise the level of water on the other side; that is their entire function. What is in view in conferring this power, I think, is the protection of the country on the side of the river opposite to that where the obstructions are made, from alterations in the level of the water. There is no purpose of protecting the rights of the country on the other side in the navigation of the channels. Manifestly the power of the commissioners is limited Mr. DOHERTY.
to judging cases where the level of the water opposite the side where the obstruction has been created, is altered, and does not extend to determining to what extent the rights of navigation on the part of one party may be affected by the construction made upon the other side. This is made clear by the preamble of this treaty which says what the purpose of the treaty itself is. [DOT] The purpose of the treaty is clearly not to alter any situations which are settled and fixed by previous treaties. I need not say that there is no safer guide to correct interpretation than that which is set forth in the preamble of the Bill. What is the purpose of this treaty? The preamble tells us that.
His Majesty, the King and the United States of America, being equally desirous to prevent disputes regarding the use of boundary waters and to settle all questions which are now pending between the United Stales and the Dominion of Canada involving f he rights, obligations, or interests of either in relation to the other or to the inhabitants cf the other along their common frontier, and to make provision for the adjustment and settlement of all such questions as may hereafter arise, have resolved to conclude a treaty in furtherance of these ends.
That is to regulate the uses of the water and to determine all questions- which are now pending between the two countries. It cannot be contended that at the time of the enactment of this treaty there was any pending question with regard to the free and open navigation of these two channels. That question had been absolutely settled and concluded by the terms of the Ashburton treaty which dealt expressly and specifically with these two particular channels and created the rights of Canada in them. So, I say it is clear that there are limitations put upon the power of these commissioners under which that power is to be exercised only in cases where the flow of water is affected and clear, from the purposes for which this treaty was entered into, that the treaty was not intended to and does not alter the express provisions in the Ashburton treaty in regard to navigation; and not so altering them it clearly does not place the determination of any questions arising under the Ashburton treaty under the jurisdiction of these commissioners.
There is another reason which I think can be advanced in support of my proposition. I do not think I am making any mistake in saying fyhat in interpreting these treaties and determining the effect of them, one upCon the other, we ,are perfectly justified in applying the rules that are applied as regards the interpretation of laws and the effect of one upon another when it is a question of how far a subsequent law repeals a previous one. We-

would be justified, when construing these two treaties between these countries, in applying the rules that govern the interpretation of contracts. I urge without fear of serious contradiction that it cannot be denied that when you have made a special, particular and specific law to deal with one particular specific instance, the subsequent enactment of general provisions does not override that law. In the system under which 1 was brought up that simple rule as expressed, declared that throughout the whole law 'in toto jure' the special rule derogates from the general rule.
I do not think anybody will deny that.
Here then we have the determination of a specific case by the Ashburton treaty.
What does my hon. friend want *the amendment of my hon. friend from Grenville for?

I want it because this government stands before this parliament interpreting this treaty as governing this case and giving power to these commissioners to assent to any works which the American government might erect on that side, and because, if we pass this legislation in the face of that authoritative interpretation and without any reserve or qualification, we will be furnishing a very powerful argument to our adversaries in this matter which they will not fail to invoke when they come to claim that because they have the assent of these commissioners our parliament has absolutely nothing to do with it. I am free to confess that our position has been far from ameliorated by the terms of this treaty as expressed, but I want to, at least, as far as it is in my power, bring about the result that this particular legislation shall not make our position worse than it _ is from my point of view. Perhaps the Minister of Public Works, seeing that the Minister of Justice has disagreed with him in the interpretation, that I have not been able to agree entirely with either of them, and that the hon. member for South Toronto is in the same position, will at least admit that there may be room for doubt as to the interpretation of this clause. If that be the case surely it is not intended that this legislation should be enacted for the purposes of serving as a means of enabling an interpretation to be put upon this treaty. If we pass it purely and simply we are building up a very strong argument in -support of the interpretation put upon this treaty by the Minister of Justice, and we are placing our adversaries, if we should come to have adversaries, or if we should come to take an adverse position to that
of the government of the United States and it was to their interest to say that all they had to do was to get the assent of the commissioners under this treaty in order to bind Canada, in possession- of an additional argument in favour of such a contention. I have no very great hope of producing conviction in the mind of the Minister of Public Works, but I must say that it does seem to me tihat I am arguing in support of a most eminently reasonable position, because, if the view of those who desire to propose this amendment to this section in respect to which there are disputed interpretations should prove to be wrong, then the amendment will have done absolutely no harm; whereas, if, in the face of this clause, susceptible of different interpretations, the amendment should be accepted, it will do this much good that it will leave that section absolutely to be interpreted as it ought to be interpreted according to the proper rules of interpretation without that internretation being affected in the slightest degree by this legislation. * Unless it is intended 'by this legislation that parliament should intervene for the purpose of interpreting this treaty and interpreting it in a sense favourable towards those with whom we made this bargain, unless it is desired that we should add to this treaty and to its terms an authoritative interpretation favourable to the persons with whom we are dealing in the event of there coming up a difference of opinion between us, it seems to me that there can be no reasonable objection to adopting this amendment proposed by my hen. friend from Grenville, and which, I think, is a valuable section as, at all events, insuring this country against the action we are taking now being interpreted as impairing in any way its rights such as they actually are under this treaty, or as, I believe, they are under the Ashburton treaty.

I would not for a moment think of setting up my views against the opinion of the Minister of Justice which no doubt is the correct one. On the point that this treaty does not give any right to the commissioner to interfere with navigation, there is no doubt. My hon. friend (Mr. Doherty) who has made a very able argument takes that ground.
The minister does not.

I did not understand the Minister of Justice to argue that this treaty in any way interferes with the Ashburton treaty. Article I of this _ treaty clearly preserves the right of navigation in substantially the language of the Ashburton treaty. Either country can make improvements, but these improvements

must always be aids and improvements to navigation, and the commissioners would have no power to give any consent to any obstruction which would interfere with the free navigation of that part of the St. Lawrence. This makes it absolutely clear that the amendment of my hon. friend (Mr. Reid) is not required. Then in section 12 of the Act of last session it is provided that no plans, no proposition, no application to the British government even to alter the terms of the Ashburton treaty can be made without the approval of the parliament of Canada. The amendment of the hon. gentleman could not safeguard the rights of our people better than they are safeguarded now.
The Minister of Public Works stated that the language of this treaty was exactly the same as the language*of the Ashburton treaty.
I said it was substantially the same. -
Article 7 of the Ashburton treaty says that channels in the River St. Lawrence on both sides of the Long Sault and Barnhart Island shall be equally free to the ships of both nations.
And this says boundary waters.
The clause in this treaty means free passage through the canals when they are built.
Is not that the same as the Ashburton treaty?

If this dam is built there will be only one channel where there are two now, because the north channel which is the main channel now on the downward route, will be spoiled. When this Bill was before Congress there was strong opposition to that feature, from amongst others the city of Montreal, the Board of Trade, the Chambre de Commerce, the Harbour Commissioners, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, the Citizens' Association, the Canadian Shipping Federation, the Montreal Transportation Company, the Richelieu and Ontario Navigation Company, the town of Morrisburg and the city of Toronto. Here we have able lawyers disagreeing on the construction of that clause and yet the Minister of Public Works refuses to insert a clause which makes the meaning plain beyond doubt.
If the Minister of Public Works wants to protect the interests of the people of Canada, he will surely put in that clause. This whole scheme with regard to the Long Sault is sure to come up again, and I think it is dangerous to leave it where there is a possible chance of doubt. I think he should not object to that clause being added, and Mr. PUGSLEY.
then the Bill would go along, and we would be able to hurry the business through. Surely the minister cannot think that in asking that there is any obstruction; the object is simply to make plain the clause. On the other side of the line, when this Bill was before Congress, Mr. Maltby, the gentleman acting for the company that was trying to get the Bill through, was asked at the end of the hearing by Chairman Burton of the special committee, if it was contemplated to go on with the construction of the dam without the consent of the government of Canada, and he admitted that it was. So evidently they do not intend to carry out the treaty, and I think the minister should consider that. Now, I want to correct one thing that the minister stated in the early part of this discussion, when he denied that he had said that he would protect Canada by collecting from the company $30,000 or $35,000 a year for the privilege. 'Here is what happened, on page 917 of ' Hansard ':

When we raised the question of damming the St. Lawrence the hon. minister made the statement that he was protecting the interests of Canada because we were going to get $30,000 a yean of revenue from that, similar to what the United States was getting.
_ Mr. PUGSLEY. What I stated was that if parliament should hereafter grant any authority to dam the St. Lawrence and I were Minister of Publio Works at the time, I would see that any company getting the power would pay as much as was to be paid to the state of New York, which I understood was to be $30,000 a year.

That is, if parliament was hereafter to grant the right. What the hon. gentleman said was that I was in favour of granting the right subject to a rental of so much a year. I said that I had made no such statement, and what the hon. gentleman has read absolutely confirms what I said.

I would like to ask, for information, if we pass this Bill confirming the treaty, could a company or an individual, under Article 3, get the right from the United States government to dam the St. Lawrence, and then only require to get the consent of this Joint Commission to go on with the work, regardless of whether it altered the level of the water or not? If we pass this Bill, then under clause (3) of the treaty any company or individual getting the right from the United States government to dam the St. Lawrence could go on and do so, and if that dam altered the level of the water on the other side, the consent of the Joipt Commission would have to be obtained.

As regards the construction of works on the United States

side which would in any way affect the level of the waters on the Canadian side, this treaty does not apply at all. In respect of the St. Lawrence, the Ashburton treaty still exists; and it is provided by that treaty and also by article (1) of this treaty that there must be free navigation preserved to the people of both countries.

I only use the St. Lawrence as an illustration. I want the interpretation of the government on clause (3). As I understand that clause, parties desiring to construct works in either country must get the consent of the parliament of the country in which the works are to be constructed; but if the work affects the boundary waters in the other country, the parties must get in addition the consent of the Joint Commission.
Yes.
And no further consent? '
If they affect navigation, the works could not be constructed at all under article (1). That article provides that navigation of all boundary waters must be kept free.

But if a company got the consent of its own government to construct a dam which might interfere with the flow of water on the other side of the boundary, they would have to get this consent of the Joint Commission.
You mean on the other side of the line?

Suppose a company desires to construct a dam on the American side, they would naturally get the consent of their own government. But if that dam would affect the level of the water on our side, they would have also to get the consent of the Joint Commission, and that would be all they would require.
Subject always to article (1) which provides that all boundary waters shall be kept open to navigation freely to the people of both countries.

The treaty and more especially the Bill deal very largely with the public domain of the provinces, especially of Ontario, and the provincial laws are to be apparently abrogated or overridden wherever they interfere with the operation of this treaty. Has the government conferred in any way with the province of Ontario, both as regards the appropriation of public waterways and the overriding of provincial laws, and has the province of Ontario given its consent to this measure? As has been pointed out to-night, although this Bill has been on the. Order Paper for a considerable length of time, the treaty has been over two years
in operation. Only the other day a Bill was brought down by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) for the purpose of putting into operation this treaty and providing machinery including a very large expenditure of ways and means. That Bill went to the public but it has since been very largely amended.
All those sections remain just as they were.
As regards the overriding of provincial laws, I think that section of the Bill is entirely new, and I do not know if the provinces are aware of this change.

None of the provinces were consulted in the framing of the treaty. All that section (2) of the Bill provides is that, so far as may be necessary to carry out the provisions of the treaty, all Dominion and provincial law's shall be altered. The only respect in which they can be altered would be as to the remedies given to people in the adjoining country to bring actions in the Exchequer Court for damages on account of injuries sustained by reason of the diversion of the water. Provision is made for the issuing of subpoena and the taking of evidence under oath. Any effect which this Bill would have upon provincial laws would be only such as is necessary to put in force the provisions of this treaty. The limitation is contained in clause (2).

That contains no limit whatever.
The section is as follows:
The laws of Canada and of the several provinces thereof are hereby amended and altered so as to permit, authorize and sanction the performance of the obligations undertaken by His Majesty in and under the said treaty; and so as to sanction, confer and impose the various rights, duties and disabilities intended by the said treaty to be conferred or imposed or to exist within Canada.
Limited wholly to the necessary connection with the treaty.
At one fell swoop it is proposed to amend all the law's of all the provinces so as to permit this treaty to have full operation and effect.
That is so.

Having regard to the public domain, surely the minister does not consider that because waters are international or boundary waters, they cease to be provincial waters. I do not think there is legal authority for any such proposition. In as much as this treaty proposes not only to deal with international or boundary waters, but to extend its operation to waters very remote from the boundary or international waters-waters that are notoriously

provincial waters-it seems to me that when we come to the wide power given by section 2, you simply propose (if you have the right to pass that section 2) that for treaty purposes and Dominion purposes, the domain of the various provinces where it comes in contact with this treaty, shall be included under the Act. I will just point out the far-reaching effect of the language used. Take, for instance, article 1. Therein we find these waters defined, and they not only include boundary waters but waters connected with boundary waters, and also, by the preliminary article, ' all bays, arms and inlets thereof, &c.'
