This would include the Georgian bay and all the waters tributary to it. I believe the Minister of Public Works himself was authority for the statement this afternoon that because a river in Maine, flowing entirely in the state of Maine, entered the St. John river, it also was a boundary water, and included in the treaty.
It is not a boundary water, but one that flows into a boundary water.

Yes, and therefore comes under the operation of the treaty. If that be so, having reference to the geographical aspect of the watershed of the Great Lakes and the. watershed of the Georgian bay, all the streams that flow into the Great Lakes and Georgian Bay from the north-and almost all that flow into the Great Lakes, except the Rainy river, flow in from the north, that, from Canadian territory-according to this definition, at one fell swoop
The hon. gentleman has not read it. It expressly excludes all tributary waters.
Then, why did the minister include the river of which he spoke?
That is different. I was speaking with reference to what was done as to the Allegash.

Then, it either is or is not a boundary water. And take section 2 of article 1. It extends not only to natural bodies of water, but ' to all canals connecting boundary waters and now existing or which may hereafter be constructed on either side of the line.' The effect of this- speaking subject to correction and simply as a matter of common reading of English- that if we construct the Georgian Bay canal, forming part of the Ottawa river, that tribu-Mr. MACDONELL.
tary for 300 or 400 miles will be held under the treaty in common. So, by this joint commission we submit to the joint supervision of the United States and ourselves all the inland waters and canals belonging to the Dominion of Canada.
Where did the hon. gentleman find that in the treaty, it must be a canal connecting boundary waters.

I am glad the hon. gentleman has mentioned that. Lake Huron is a boundary water, and Georgian bay, by the preliminary article, is a part of a boundary water, because it is a bay that is included in ' all bays, arms and inlets thereof.' So the Georgian bay canal, which goes to the Georgian bay, which is part of the boundary waters-
And joins the St. Lawrence where it has ceased to be boundary water.
It flows from boundary waters, and it joins boundary waters.
No, it joins the St. Lawrence below where it is a boundary water.
The St. Lawrence is a boundary stream.
Only to a certain point.
You will find that our American friends will claim the whole length.
No.

There is the fact staring you in the face. It seems to me that the rights of the provinces have been overlooked, and that there has been no attempt to safeguard those rights or consult the provinces in the confiscation or disposal of their rights. The minister is well aware of the decision in the fishery case in the Privy Council. It is common knowledge that it was decided' that the Dominion government has no right in the waters except where they have been improved in rivers, harbours, or canals, but that public waters and land under public waters, in the old province of Canada, belong either to the province of Ontario or to the province of Quebec. And you will find nowhere in the British North America Act any authority to divest the province of Ontario of its domain in these waters or under them. Yet this measure proposes to deal with them without even consulting the provinces. Then you have the additional feature that, as I have said, at one fell swoop, you wipe out provincial legislation that is in conflict with the operation of this treaty. Every lawyer knows-the Minister of Justice (Sir Allen Aylesworth), is not here, but if he were here I am sure he would agree with me-

that of all legislation, legislation by inference or reference is the most obnoxious. To declare generally that all law in conflict with what is here laid down shall be amended, altered, or repealed, is the most objectionable kind of legislation, because you have to go to court every time you want to find out what the rights of the individual are, and to what extent these laws are altered, amended, or require to be altered, amended, or repealed, to be in conformity with the treaty. So, both the contents of the Bill, and the manner in which it is brought down-without consultation with the parties vitally interested -are objectionable. It does seem to me that the objection raised by the hon. member for Grenville (Mr. Reid), has been well taken. The amendment can do no harm if inserted. I might point out here that in the case before the committee of the Senate of the United States with regard to the erection of an obstruction in the St. Lawrence it was there openly stated that the effect of allowing that legislation to go through would be to entirely abrogate those clauses in the Ashburton treaty which require the River St. Lawrence to be forever free and clear. If the Minister of Public Works should accept the amendment of the member for Grenville, as 1 have said, its presence in the Bill would do no harm, whereas it would wonderfully safeguard the rights of the people of this country, and make plain, and unequivocal the position which we all, the minister included, agree should be taken, namely, that it is not in any way intended or desired to interfere with the freedom of the river which has been guaranteed by the provisions of the Ashburton treaty. 1 think the minister would do well to consider whether he should not accept that amendment. The minister has made some remarks about not making headway with the Bill. That is his own fault- in not bringing down this impprtiant measure until practically on the eve of adjournment. If this Bill had been brought down long ago, it could have had more consideration.
I have delayed it frequently at the special request of hon. gentlemen opposite who were desirous of being present. However, I do not complain.

This treaty has been in operation now for more than two years. The provision for financing the commission is a matter that can go on. In answer to a question I put the government, I was informed that the government has spent already $218,329 on the Waterways Commission.
Not this commission, that is under the old treaty.

It is the same men and the same work. However, there has been a large amount expended already. If this Bill were not passed the expenditure could go on. In the meantime the minister would do well to let this measure stand for further mature consideration until after the adjournment. We find the Minister of Public Works holding one view, and the Minister of Justice another view, but the Bill goes on all the same. I think it would be in the interests of the country to let this measure stand, and let the government consult with the provinces who are affected by it. The rights of the provinces are being impaired by this Bill, both in regard to their public domain, and to their public law. It would be better for the government to wait awhile, and come to some arrangement with the provinces for taking joint action.

If the Americans got a Bill through at Washington giving them power to dam the South Sault, then all they would want would be the consent of the Joint Commission. Would the Minister of Public Works take that position?

What I have said already is that this treaty gives no right whatever to dam the St. Lawrence river, or any other river; on the contrary, it preserves every right of navigation. Article 1 declares that the navigation of all navigable boundary waters shall forever continue free and open for the purpose of commerce to the inhabitants of both countries, safeguarding to the fullest extent the right of navigation:	In the case my
hon. friend put of the United States Congress giving authority to place a dam upon their own side of the boundary, this treaty gives no such power. That is a power which they have at the present time, but this treaty contains a prohibitive clause which says that they shall not do that, if the effect is to raise the water level upon the Canadian side, without the consent of the International Joint Commission. While Canada might erect works on its own side, if the effect was to alter the level of the water on the other side of the boundary, there must be the consent of the International Joint Commission. This treaty gives no power to place an obstruction of any kind or description in a boundary water; on the contrary, it limits the right which exists at the present time. It preserves every right of navigation, and provides also that if the parliament of either country should authorize the construction of any works, they must be subject to every right of navigation, and must always be subject to the approval of the International Joint Commission, if the level of the water on the other side of the boundary is affected.

This treaty has been in operation for over a year, and why is it that we have had so much trouble this winter trying to prevent the Long Sault (Company from1 interfering with the St. Lawrence? We have made representations from this House over and over again, the city of Montreal has been much exercised over it, and representations have been made to Washington, and the attention of the commission has been drawn to it, notwithstanding the fact that under this treaty they could not interfere with it in any way.

The minister knows that at Washington they have been fighting all winter, and Congress did not hesitate to say they had the right. But, as I understand it from what the Minister of Public Works said, they can erect a dam in the South Sault, and all they want is the consent of the Joint Commission.

Before this treaty was negotiated Congress could authorize, the same as the Canadian parliament could authorize works, each upon its own side of the boundary. This treaty limits that right because it makes all subject to free navigation.

They probably could if it had not been for the Ashburton treaty which provides that the channels on both sides, the Long Sault and Barnhart Island, should remain free and open. These are the two channels mentioned there.

Does not my hon. friend understand clearly, as the hon. member for Montreal, Ste. Anne said, that the Ashburton treaty is in no way affected by this treaty. It remains as it is and as it will always remain providing for the free and unobstructed navigation of these channels. This treaty goes even farther and says that in all the boundary waters there shall be that free right of navigation.
I cannot see it in that light.
If my hon. friend will not take my view he might take the view of the hon. member for Montreal, Ste. Anne.

The minister made the statement a few minutes ago that he had delayed this Bill at the request of members on this side of the House and he said that on one occasion I asked him to hold it over from Friday to Monday. I plead guilty to that.
I would be very glad to hold it over at any time for hon. members.
That is the only time that I remember.
The hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Magrath) also requested me to hold it over.

This Bill in its changed form was only handed around this morning and I would ask the minister if he would allow it to stand over until tomorrow in order that we may really understand it and then it can go through.
I think the hon. members clearly understand the Bill.

I am not quite sure of that. I think it is only fair to ask that it be allowed to stand over. There are other members who have not been here and who have not seen this Bill. They should have an opportunity of seeing it and the minister should not desire to force it through.
These new clauses are all unimportant.
It is not a matter of any consequence, hut I would like to know from the minister when I asked him to hold this Bill over.
I do not think my hon. friend did it personally but an hon. member of the House said that the hon. member for Medicine Hat was desirous of speaking on the Bill.
I wished to know when it was coming up.
I think the hon. member was away.

Can the minister tell us to what extent the Chicago Drainage canal will reduce the depth of water in the lakes? There is an enlargement and it is said to be drawing more water from Lake Michigan at 10,000 cubic feet per second, which was supposed to be the amount they should be allowed to take under the arrangement made by the commission.
I am not able to give my hon. friend definite information on that point. I understood they had the right to draw 10,000 cubic feet per second. I have not heard that that has been increased.
Has that been settled by any treaty arrangement?
No, it is by an understanding. Of course, all the cities bordering on the lakes are just as much interested in it as we are. There is no clause relating to this in the treaty.
They cannot take more than 10,000 cubic feet per second without the consent of the commission provided for in this treaty?
I am not prepared to
Can the minister inform the committee whether it is intended to make a further abstraction of water from Lake Erie by. the enlargement of the Erie canal?

I have not heard of anything of the kind. Of course, there is work going on now with the view of deepening the Erie canal. I may say to my hon. friend that the water that is used for filling a canal is not very likely to appreciably alter the level of the great lakes. We should not raise that question at all events. What might more seriously alter the levels would be the deepening of the canal through the St. Clair Flats, although that is for the joint benefit of both countries.
-Mr. REID (Grenville). Suppose the Long Sault were to be dammed what effect would it have on the lakes on the eastern side of it? The River St. Lawrence goes into a lake east of the town of Cornwall; and what would be the result if this commission should grant power to dam the St. Lawrence.
This commission cannot grant power to dam the St. Lawrence.
Well there is a difference of opinion.

This treaty does not give power to dam the St. Lawrence.
On section 4: Exchequer Court jurisdiction.

I would like to ask the minister why it is considered necessary to give this jurisdiction to the Exchequer Court? In our own province of Quebec, if a man diverted the waters of a stream running in the province of Quebec, and crossing the boundary, and thereby did damage to a man in the state of Maine, he would, under the treaty, become liable towards that man in the state of Maine just precisely to the same extent as he would under the law of the province of Quebec be liable to his next door neighbour for a like diversion of the same stream. In other words the liability of the party guilty of the offence which gives rise to the damage is to be governed by the law of the province of Quebec. The province has created courts for the administration of justice, and I can see no reason why you should take the party defendant before a court which as a general rule has no jurisdiction to administer the law of the province. I am not attempting to reflect in the slightest degree upon the gentleman who is now judge of the Exchequer Court, but in the province of Quebec it is known that we have a distinct system of law, under which the obligations of the man who diverts the stream as well as the rights of the man injured will be governed. The
provincial courts are especially created for the administration of that law, are presided over by men trained in that law, and you will draw these cases from their jurisdiction and give them to a tribunal which as a rale is not concerned with the administration of that law. Then in that province you will very probably have the language question. I am not now making any personal reference, but it will likely happen that the judge of the Exchequer Court will not be familiar with the French and English languages, and in Quebec the two languages are official, and the people attach considerable importance to their right to be heard in their own tongue. Apart from sentimental consideration those who have experience in these courts know how exceedingly important it is in the interests of justice that the witnesses should be heard by a judge who understands both languages. In the province of Quebec, in nine cases out of every ten, the bulk of the cases are in the French language, and it is rare to have a case in which both parties, and the counsel, and the witnesses speak only English. I am at a loss to see why you should create this exceptional jurisdiction to deal with cases of this kind which affect civil Tights that belong to the jurisdiction of the province. I urge upon the consideration of the government that justice would probably be much more satisfactorily attained by leaving the adjudication of these cases to the courts to which they naturally belong.

I do not think it is of very great importance what court a suppliant may enter in order to get redress, the important thing being to let him know what court he has a right to go to, and be assured that that court has jurisdiction. I suppose that one reason for providing the Exchequer Court would be that all actions taken under this treaty would be of the same character, and it would be desirable that one tribunal should deal with them.

If the liability for diverting a stream should be different in one province under the law of that province from what it would be in another province, the cases would not be of the same kind or under the same law.

At all events, they will all be cases of damages in relation to watercourses and boundary waters. In the province of Quebec, I imagine, there will not be many cases, and the present judge of the Exchequer Court speaks both languages, as I apprehend any judge would who would be likely to be appointed. I know that Mr. Justice Burbidge spoke French very well, having studied it after he became a judge, and Mr. Justice Cassels speaks French

very well. The judge of the Exchequer Court travels about from one place to another, and would be willing to go to any town or city where the parties lived to try the cases. The Exchequer Court would perhaps be the best court to which to give jurisdiction in the cases provided for under this treaty. If after practical experience it is found desirable to make a change, it can he made in the future. I trust that my hon. friend will not press for a change, but allow the section to go through as it is.

I do not wish to press unduly; but while section 132 of the British North America Act makes it clear that this parliament has power to pass any law to give effect in any province to any rights created under the treaty, it seems to me that in the exercise of that power we ought to try to interfere as little as possible with the rights of the provinces. This is a part of the administration of justice in the provinces, even though it results from a law that we pass. It is not the treaty that makes the law of Quebec what previously was not the law of Quebec, but it is in virtue of this enactment that it becomes law. Why depart from the application of the general rule that the administration of justice belongs to the province? As a matter of principle, it seems to me that we ought, under section 132 of the British North America Act, to confine ourselves to doing what it provides we shall do, that is, enact the laws which are necessary to give effect to these rights that we create, and then leave the administration of those laws to the provinces. It is not at all necessary, in order to give effect to these rights, that we should create a special court for this privileged class of plaintiffs. I accept the statement of the hon. member in regard to the two judges of the Exchequer Court speaking both languages; I do not want to make any personal observations about any judge, past or present; but I think lawyers front the province of Quebec will bear me out in saying that there have been cases in which it was the subject of serious complaint that before the tribunal mentioned the parties were not in a position to be heard in their own language. When you have an entirely organized system that meets a desire, and a not unreasonable desire, on the part of persons speaking a particular language to be given a court where their language would be official, a court which would without doubt be qualified to hear and understand testimony if it should be given in that language, it is at least remarkable that you should provide a court 'which may possibly be in a position where it would be necessary to interpret all this testimony. Moreover, the procedure in these cases will be governed by the Code of Civil Procedure in the province of Quebec. I see no provision to Mr. PUGSLEY.
the contrary in the Bill. It does seem to me that all these considerations ought to weigh against something which is a departure from general rules, and in support of which I have not heard any very substantial reasons. It seems to me that if we say to the foreigner, you shall have the .game recourse as any citizen of Canada, and have it before the same court, we shall be implementing our obligations under the treaty to the full, and leaving him in no doubt as to what court he should go before.
This section was drafted by the Justice Department, and the matter does not seem to me to be Of sufficient importance to make a change in it.
Perhaps I might take the liberty of asking the Solicitor General whether these considerations which I have ventured to offer were thought of before this was enacted.
It came from the Deputy Minister of Justice.

I do not know that it would be any reflection on the department to suggest that possibly these matters nad not been thought of, and it would be more satisfactory if when one has grounds for suggesting a change he should have the gratification of feeling that the author of the Act had given them some consideration. It is an unfortunate condition, when one urges reasons before the minister who is responsible for the Bill, to be told that this has been decided by somebody else who is not here to listen to you and to whom possibly these considerations did not occur.
I would like to ask the minister whether the commission to be anpointed under this Act will [DOT]have any jurisdiction on the St. Lawrence from the boundary line at Cornwall down to Montreal?
I think not. That is wholly in Canadian waters, and the commission is limited to boundary waters.
Then we have the sole jurisdiction over the canal from the Georgian bay to Montreal, and the United States would not be entitled to the user?
No.
Although they have the right to navigate the St. Lawrence by treaty, that onlv applies from boundary waters to boundary waters?
Perfectly correct.
This only gives power to navigate jointly as far as Cornwall?

This treaty is confined to boundary waters.

On section 5,
The International Joint Commission, when appointed and constituted pursuant to the said treaty, shall have power, when holding joint sessions in Canada, to take evidence on oath and to compel the attendance of witnesses by application to a judge of a superior court of the province within which such session is held, and such judge is hereby authorized and directed to make all orders and issue all processes necessary and appropriate to that end.
Is there provision made for the payment of fees to witnesses?

Yes, these would be included in the expenses of the commission.
On section 6,
The Governor in Council may appropriate annually, out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund, a sum not exceeding seventy-five thousand dollars, toward the payment of the salaries of the commissioners to be appointed by His Majesty on the recommendation of the Governor in Council, as well as the salaries of the secretary and other officers and employees, and also all other expenses which may be incurred by such commissioners with the approval of the Minister of Public Works, together with one-half share of all reasonable and necessary joint expenses of the said commission incurred by it and, under the terms of the said treaty, required to be paid in equal moieties by the High Contracting Parties.

It seems to me that we are doing many things which are not correct. Our salary list is subject every year to discussion in Committee of Supply, and we have no right to fix the salaries in. a Bill of this kind.

In the case of the Board of Railway Commissioners, their salaries are fixed by statute. In appointing gentlemen to a very important position such as this, particularly when the treaty runs for a term of years they would naturally want to know what their salaries would be. I thought that parliament would prefer that a limit should be put on the salaries.
This parliament has no right to bind another parliament. The principle that obtains in matters of that kind is for parliament from year to year to fix the expenditure.
The judges' salaries are fixed by statute, and not by vote from year to year.	,

It may be Teasonble to fix the judges' salaries, _ but it is a wrong principle to embody in a statute payments that ought to be voted by this House.
On section 7,
Each of the said commissioners who is appointed by His Majesty shall receive as compensation for his services an amount to be fixed by the Governor in Council but not in excess of the sum paid by the government of the United States to each of its commissioners, and not in any case to exceed the sum of seventy-five hundred dollars per annum. The secretary appointed by the Canadian section of the commission under the provisions of tile said treaty shall receive as compensation for his services a sum not exceeding three thousand dollars per annum.

I think that these words, * not in excess of the sum paid by the government of the United States ' should be struck out. I can see no reason why the salaries of these commissioners should be governed by any allowances the United. States may make.- We ought to be able to determine ourselves what their services are worth, and we should pay what they are worth.

In the appropriation Act passed at Washington, it is provided that the salaries to be paid the commissioners in the United States shall not be greater than those paid by the government of Canada. It is very desirable that both countries should pay the same salaries as these commissioners are sitting together and doing the same work. The idea is that the commissioners on both sides be paid the same salaries.
When do the governments of the two countries get together to fix what the sum is to be?
When this statute is passed, in the ordinary course we would get together and fix the salaries.
Are the ministers going to have another mission to Washington to get that settled? I suppose it will be arranged that the Canadian Commissioner is to have the same bill of fare as the American.
Ought to have better.

How would the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) like to have the same rule applied to his department? If it were applied he would be giving the chief of the management of the Intercolonial railway $50,000 a year.
That is a comparison of salaries, one paid by a private company and the other by a government road, but in this other case both are working for governments.
That is a nice way to put it. It seems to- me that the governments take the position: * After you

my dear Alfonse,' ' After you my dear Gaston.' The result will be that you will have to have another Joint Commission to fix the salaries of these gentlemen. I think it is childish to put such a provision in a Bill dealing with an international question.

This is a very serious innovation. The reason a statutory allowance is given the judges is to provide against their removal except by impeachment. If you could stop a judge's sakiry you would in effect dismiss him from office without impeaching him. But statutory allowances are only given to judges, railway commissioners and a few others who are appointed during good behaviour and cannot be removed except for good reason.
What about the penitentiary officials. Their salaries are regulated by statute. You cannot exceed the amount mentioned in the statute.

But their salaries as I understand, are voted every year. The principle applies only to parties who are removable by impeachment. The minister (Mr. Pugsley) refers to the United States. But the United States will never commit the folly of passing a statute fixing the salaries of these parties; they will vote the salaries every year. Why do not we do the same, so that the House of Commons can control them?

I am willing to take the suggestion of my hon. friend from Digby (Mr. Jameson), and strike out the words ' but not in excess of the sum paid by the government of the United States.' I move that these words be struck out.
Will the commissioners be expected to devote their whole time to the service of the commission?

That has not yet been decided. My own opinion is that if they receive the maximum salary provided for in the section, they ought to devote their whole time to the work of the commission. Of course, it may be desirable to engage the services of some gentleman who might have other work to do, and who would be paid by the day or paid a smaller sum than that fixed by this Bill. But, in case the salary should be the same, or nearly the same as is provided in the Bill, I think they should give their whole time to the work of the commission.
What are the salaries ' now paid to the commissioners?
The chairman gets $50 a day, and the other commissioners $25 a day, for the time actually engaged in the work of the commission.

I think that the point raised by the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Haggart) is well taken. The minister knows that there are two kinds of appointments under the Crown, one continuing as long as the appointee's conduct is proper. Such appointee is not removable except by impeachment, really at the bar of this House. But other appointments are during pleasure, and I understand that the salaries of these appointees simply appear in the Supply Bill. I do not think the principle here proposed should be embodied in legislation pertaining to a treaty. It is only for five years; it is not a life appointment. The whole thing could be adjusted without such an enactment. It involves a vicious principle.

The amount is not fixed, and the Governor in Council is to fix it. But once he exercises that power I doubt very much if he can reduce it-it becomes a statutory enactment under which they are entitled to their pay.

I think undoubtedly-that is so.
Amendment (Mr. Pugsley) agreed to, and section 7 as amended agreed to.
Next we -come to the schedule and protocols. I think every hon. member has read this because it has been before parliament

Before that is taken up, I wish to move as section 8 the amendment which I submitted before.
Amendment negatived.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.

Mr. FIELDING moved that the House go into Committee of the Whole to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to amend chapter 31, Revised Statutes, The Penny Bank Act, and by such amendment authorize the Minister of Finance to fijx and determine the rate of interest that shall be allowed and credited half-yearly on the amounts from time to time at the credit of the accounts of penny banks, incorporated under the provisions of that Act, in the government savings bank or post office savings bank, the rate so fixed and determined not to exceed one per centum in advance of the rate then payable to depositors in the government savings bank or post office savings bank.
He said: This resolution is to enable us to increase the allowance to Penny Banks by one-half per cent. Several public spirited gentlemen in Toronto, a few years ago, initiated a movement f.or the encouragement of thrift by establishing what is

called the Penny Bank. Since that time another bank of similar character has been established at Chicoutimi in the province of Quebec. All the money that is collected is placed in the government savings bank, except a very small amount as working capital which remains in the hands of the Penny Bank. We have been allowing them three and a half per cent, while they allow the depositors three per cent. In order to assist them with the expenses of management we propose to increase the allowance to one per cent above the savings bank rate instead of a half per cent. At present it represents an increased allowance of about $780 per annum. It is to help them with the expenses of management. At the beginning the expenses were borne by some public spirited citizens, but since then some of these have dropped off. As we think the movement is deserving of encouragement, we propose to give them one per cent instead of a half per cent.
This work for the Penny Banks is done largely by the school teachers of the city of Toronto. They do not get anything for that work.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, I do not think the school teachers get anything. Experience has shown that it is a very desirable thing. The gentlemen who are promoting it are public spirited citizens who put their own money into it to a considerable degree.

Motion agreed to, and House went into Committee on the Resolution.
Resolution reported, read the second time and agreed to.
Mr. FIELDING moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 221) to amend the Penny Bank Act.
Motion agreed to, Bill read the first and second time, considered in committee, reported, read the third time, and passed.

On section 2,
I notice that this Bill does not deal with the saving banks in Quebec.

speechtext:
I have a separate Bill in relation to those, which is now passing through the House, and I will be very happy to move it to-morrow.
On the preamble,
If the minister will agree to allow the third reading to stand over-I have no objection to this Bill, but I want an opportunity of reading it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am quite content to accept my hon. friend's suggestion.

Bill (No. 211) respecting aid towards the construction of the Canadian Northern Ontario Railway-Mr. Graham-read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.

This Bill is identical with the resolution that we discussed the other day, and to which we made one amendment at the suggestion of the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax). In a Bill of this kind there cannot be much diversion from the original resolution. I do not want to press it unduly, but it is identical in its terms with the resolution we passed the other day. If we could take a few minutes and uo through a portion of it, we would be able to give it to the Senate before they adjourn.
The minister was to give some explanation of the securities on that part of the road from Montreal to the Niagara river.

My information is that they are allowed to issue $30,000 'a mile. With respect to the securities between Montreal and a point opposite Hawkesbury there was a subsidy voted by this parliament, but it has not as yet been paid or earned. been acquired by the Canadian Northern will come under the second mortgage, but they will remain branch lines. That piece of road which will form part of the main line is to be reconstructed up to standard.
This Bill has been advanced an important stage to-night and in the absence of the leader of the opposition, I move that the committee rise.

There is no need to move that. I said that if any one objected when we got to the second reading we would not proceed. It is an important Bill, but if we are going to get through as hon. gentlemen want, we will have to work hard, and sit late.

We have been fourteen hours at it to-day, and the Minister of Labour is trying to get through an eight hour Bill.
Progress reported.
Mr. FIELDING moved the adjournment of the House.

speechtext: The Canadian Northern Bill, the Railway Act, the resolutions respecting trade with Japan, and we would like to have the Grain Bill advanced a stage.
